SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed from November 5 consideration of the motion that this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government, of the amendment and of the amendment to the amendment.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Honoré-Mercier.

As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, it gives me great honour to rise today to speak to budget 2026. Yesterday, the Minister of Finance rose in the chamber to deliver budget 2026, an ambitious yet common-sense plan that would build on the generational investments made in budget 2025 to grow our economy, protect our communities and build a more unified Canada.

As Canada grapples with this unique moment in history, it is important to remember that Canada has what the world wants and the foundations to build more ourselves here at home: abundant energy, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, leadership in AI and extraordinary talent all across this country. Unlike those who talk the economy down, talk down our workers or claim that Canada is broken, budget 2026 will harness our strengths here at home and help Canadian businesses invest, improve productivity, scale up at home, compete on the world stage and create good-paying jobs.

This budget will show that Canada is moving, and moving fast, to build a strong, more resilient and more united country, and while that long-term vision takes root, we will provide Canadians with a bridge and a boost in the interim to help make life more affordable. We have more than can ever be taken away from us, and budget 2026 is our plan to be the masters of our own destiny.

Budget 2026 highlights Canada's resilience amid global uncertainty. It also makes clear that Canada is meeting those challenges from a position of strength. The global economic order is experiencing its most consequential transformation in close to a century. The conflict in the Middle East has driven up energy prices. That is incontestable. Protectionism is rising around the world. Supply chains are being reorganized around security and sovereignty, and capital is seeking countries that can offer stability, energy and resources, talent, and trusted access to global markets. We have the opportunity, and in fact the duty, to meet this moment by helping to build a stronger, more independent Canadian economy.

Budget 2026 is key to that approach, and it meets the moment. While others offer slogans or partisan rhetoric, we have the right plan and we know it is working. There are many signs of progress. They are multiple and are outlined in budget 2026 in the fiscal outlook.

The world has changed dramatically. The relationships that powered Canada's prosperity for decades can no longer be taken as a given. Since we were elected, our response has been very clear: We will focus on what we can control, and we will do so from a position of strength and resilience.

We are strengthening our foundations here at home, diversifying our partnerships abroad and making life more affordable for Canadians. Our competitive advantages are among the strongest in the world, ranging from a skilled workforce, clean and traditional energy, and an abundance of critical minerals and natural resources, to our strong public finances and access to global markets. We have what the world wants, and we have what it takes to chart our own course. Canada and Canadians are ready to embrace this opportunity. We will not listen to those who say it is not possible and that we should settle for less.

The numbers show that Canada is facing these challenges from a position of strength. Canada is not immune to geopolitical realignments, but we are moving decisively to seize the opportunities that they create.

The Canadian economy grew by 3.3% annualized in the second quarter of this year, the fastest growth in the G7, driven by higher exports, household spending and new business investment. Recent data suggests that the economy remains resilient in the third quarter as well. According to the International Monetary Fund, Canada is projected to grow at the second-fastest pace in the G7 in 2027.

Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of our approach. By spending less on day-to-day operations and managing public finances responsibly, we can invest more in Canadian workers, businesses and industries while making generational investments in infrastructure, defence, housing and innovation, and increasing our productive capacity, which is needed to expand our economy. By reducing operating costs, we are also able to invest in Canada's long-term growth while making life more affordable for Canadians.

Over the past year, our government has put in place a series of ambitious strategies spanning electricity, defence, critical minerals, food security, artificial intelligence and nature. Together, they are helping Canada seize major opportunities while strengthening our resilience in a more uncertain world.

The early results are clear. Investment is growing. Major projects are advancing. New trade and investment agreements are opening markets abroad. More Canadians are finding rewarding, well-paying careers in the industries that will drive growth in the decades ahead.

Our government's strategy has helped position Canada to enter a new era of investment. Budget 2026 advances flagship tax policy changes, including the productivity mega deduction and the Canada growth incentive, which will further strengthen our tax competitiveness and create the conditions to catalyze an investment supercycle.

Through strategic, targeted investments and broad-based tax policy changes, Canada remains among the leading advanced economies for tax competitiveness. Public investment, private capital, major projects and new market opportunities are coming together to expand what Canada can build and produce for decades to come. This is at the heart of Canada's investment supercycle: a continuously evolving cycle in which each investment strengthens the conditions for the next.

Foreign direct investment in Canada is at its highest level in nearly two decades. Canada attracted $98 billion in foreign investment in 2025 and has led the G7 in direct investment inflows per capita since early 2025.

In September, Canada hosted its first-ever investment summit, bringing together approximately 200 of the world's leading investors. It helped secure nearly $500 billion in new investment commitments and financing for businesses in Canada. Our government's focus now is to turn those investment commitments into projects, jobs and growth. That means more homes, modernized infrastructure, twice the electricity capacity, new critical mineral projects, defence investments that build new industries, and deeper connections to global markets. It also means helping businesses of all sizes invest in technology, innovation, robotics and AI to boost productivity and better compete globally.

Small and medium-sized businesses are the backbone of Canada's economy, making up over 98% of Canadian businesses and creating jobs in communities across this country. To help businesses invest, grow and succeed in Canada, budget 2026 introduced several measures. They include the Canada growth incentive to help high-potential Canadian businesses attract investment and grow here at home. They also include a new tax exemption on up to $15 million in capital gains earned from successful investments in eligible Canadian companies for founders, key employees and investors, and an enhanced small business rollover to allow more investments to qualify for tax deferrals on capital gains when proceeds are reinvested in another Canadian small business.

Budget 2026 also announced a commercialization expansion of the scientific research and experimental development tax incentive program. It is worth $930 million of investment over five years to help turn more Canadian ideas into growing companies, high-paying careers and made-in-Canada innovation.

I would not do the budget justice if I did not also point to the fact that building a stronger economy means supporting Canadians with affordability. We have boosted the Canada groceries and essentials benefit and made changes to refocus the Canada workers benefit, and we are doing a lot more. We have also made the Canada caregiver credit refundable. All of these things are going to support millions of Canadians with some of the affordability challenges that we know they are feeling on a day-to-day and monthly basis.
In short, budget 2026 puts Canada in the driver's seat to determine our own future. That is exactly what Canadians hired us to do, and that is exactly what we are going to remain focused on.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague is on the finance committee with me, and we manage to work pretty well together as far as what we have to get done at that committee goes.

I heard his speech today, and I know it is a canned speech, as it always is from that side of the House, with a whole bunch of slogans. The government has been very good at coming out with marketing slogans, and I love the name of this one, “Masters of our destiny”. Masters of our own destiny includes Canadians, Canadian taxpayers and Canadian businesses, and, frankly, the government is spending their future.

There is a huge accumulation of debt in this budget classified in different ways, but we are talking about an additional $766 billion of borrowing over the next five years. It as a ludicrous amount. “Debt” is defined in public finance as demand brought forward. What is the government going to do when it has to pay that debt?
Will the member please come to the table and tell me what he means by “fiscal prudence”, because we are exactly not there, and how he is going to reiterate that line when he has to—
I have to cut off the member to allow the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance a chance to respond.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what the member has against an investment supercycle and the government stepping up to attract investment in Canada and to incentivize that investment. We are sticking to both fiscal anchors in this budget. We are getting to one of our fiscal anchors a whole year ahead of schedule.

I know the member opposite is worried about debt and debt charges. Canada has a AAA credit rating and the lowest debt service cost of the G7 countries as a result of our strong fiscal fundamentals. We also know that long-term bond yields in Canada have been largely isolated from the increases we have seen across the G7. Canada has the lowest rate of increase in bond yields of any G7 country.
Mr. Speaker, people seem to have a lot to say this morning, but you will not have to interrupt me.

In his introduction, the member said that Canada has what the world wants. That is what worries me the most, because what they are trying to do with the 6% under the superdeduction is offer a massive discount to foreign investors who want to come here to extract our natural resources and very likely, or rather certainly, process them elsewhere. That is what we call selling our natural resources at a discount.

I would like the member to explain to me how the government plans to implement measures to protect this and ensure that processing takes place here. We are all in favour of economic development, but there are limits.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has always been a jurisdiction of high standards, and we are not going to lower those standards today.

We are streamlining permitting processes to get shovels in the ground on major critical mineral projects. We have enhanced the tax deductions for exploration in this country for minerals and critical minerals and extended those benefits to incentivize more critical mineral development across Canada, because we have such a wealth of natural resource assets that the world wants and needs.

The member opposite talked about the productivity mega deduction. It cuts across the entire economy, applies to businesses of all sizes and allows them to have the confidence to invest in themselves and in new machinery and equipment and enhance their productivity after getting the tax deduction this year. That is only going to be a good thing for investment in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I think Canadians understand that at a time like this when we have to face going into deficit, we should be doing it to invest in infrastructure that will build the country for the future.

I am wondering if the member could talk a bit about the concept of separating our operating and capital expenditures and moving to try to balance the operating budget as a government over the coming years.

Mr. Speaker, that is a great question. What we have done very transparently is define a capital budgeting framework with a set of definitions that corresponds to best practices around the world. We have set ourselves up to invest in the economy, draw in and attract private capital and ensure that the economy can grow.

That is exactly what we have seen. My colleagues should remember that there is $27.5 billion less of a deficit in this budget, in this fiscal year, than was projected in the spring economic update. That is good news for this country. That is a result of growth in the economy and of new capital investment. We are seeing it rise at 9%. That is significant, and all colleagues should be able to recognize that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to highlight to the member for Calgary Centre that I will be reading my original speech today. I would also like to wish the Speaker a happy Friday. I can see that everybody appears to be in a great and jovial mood today. I suspect they are all feeling very cheerful having read yesterday's budget.
Yesterday, our government released our budget, masters in our own House or, as we say in French, Maîtres chez nous.
I would like to take the next 10 minutes to talk about an important budget.

As members know, the expression maîtres chez nous is a slogan that was used during the Quiet Revolution in Quebec. It was an expression that was used during the campaign to nationalize electricity in the 1960s, before my time. It represents our natural resources, or protecting our lakes and rivers, but it also represents protecting our culture, our identity and our pride in being Canadian.
Budget 2026 is about action, so let me outline why this budget advances many of these priorities.

Yes, the front cover of the budget includes transmission lines from Churchill Falls in Newfoundland and Labrador, and that is because electricity is at the heart of this budget. Let me go through some of those measures that would advance Canada's electricity strategy.

Budget 2026 invests $50 billion in Canada's electricity strategy, but $50 billion is more than money, though. It is about real results. New Economy Canada mentioned last night that “Budget 2026 puts electrification at the heart of Canada's economy, ensuring energy security and affordability for businesses and households.”
What would $50 billion get us? It would get us four things. First, our government's electricity strategy is about building infrastructure, because we must build really fast.

Last year, I had the honour of reading Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson's book, Abundance, which I highly recommend. This book is important because it calls for a shift toward supply-side progressivism, where the state must actively build and reform zoning and permitting laws, but invest in large-scale physical infrastructure to electrify the economy. This $50-billion investment would do that. It would electrify the economy.

When I worked in climate philanthropy, we worked with technical modelling and with partners like the Canadian Climate Institute, l'Institut de l'énergie Trottier, the David Suzuki Foundation, The Pembina Institute or The Transition Accelerator, and all modelling demonstrated that for Canada to get to net zero, we would need to at least double our electricity grid.

Yesterday's budget puts money where our mouth is. This investment in Canada's electricity strategy is about connecting grids. In a turbulent world, we need to better integrate our provinces and territories, and this includes our complex regional electricity grids.

There are 31 transmission lines that cross Canada to the U.S. border, north to south. However, to protect our sovereignty and strengthen our federation, we are now investing in integrating our grid from east to west to north. We are doing this to unify our country and to grow our economy while reducing emissions.

My third point is that our $50-billion electricity strategy is about making technological components to power our grid and build our capacity and value chains. This is a unique opportunity to advance clean-tech value chains where Canada holds a strong competitive advantage. This is an opportunity for us to advance batteries and electrochemical storage, advance electricity grid equipment and infrastructure, utilize our Canadian-made critical minerals and advance our nuclear energy with CANDU technology, but also with small modular reactors. It is also an opportunity to advance hydro, solar and wind renewable energy.

My fourth point is that our investment in electricity is about jobs and it is about labour. We need the skills and labour to help build out the grid and ensure support for great Canadian jobs across our country.

I would also like to highlight some other measures from budget 2026 that would advance Canada's electricity strategy. One, clean electricity investment tax credits phase-out to 15% would now occur in 2040 instead of 2034. This is positive news for the clean-tech sector.

Two, this budget encourages more investment in electricity transmission and does so by extending the clean electricity ITCs for provincial electricity transmission lines in each province, with $2.4 billion allocated in 2027 to 2031 and $36 billion allocated by 2042. This is about building Canada strong.

Third, it promises that $4 billion over 10 years would be provided to support electricity infrastructure expansion, renewable energy and new funding for the smart renewables and electrification pathways program.
Fourth, the budget would support robust cost-benefit analysis to better understand interties and inform cross-border cost allocation discussions.

Building out transmission lines and interties is not always a technical problem. It is often one of governance, of navigating complex provincial jurisdictions and challenges with social acceptability. According to Electricity Canada's statement last night on budget 2026, modernizing our grid is a “nation-building endeavour.”

This is about building real projects. For example, our budget would now allow the building of a 15-megawatt hydro facility in the Yukon, as well as an eight-megawatt hydro facility in Atlin. This is in addition to the massive 14,000 megawatts at Churchill Falls. We will be building more clean renewable projects for decades to come.

I spoke about grids and electricity, but let us talk about buildings and how budget 2026 benefits the decarbonization of our buildings. As Clean Energy Canada announced last night, “Budget 2026 offers a new framework for climate progress: build, switch, transform, and innovate.” Last month, our government announced a transformative $2-billion investment in a national heat pump rebate program, which will benefit one million Canadian homes and reduce 25 megatonnes of greenhouse gas emissions, while significantly reducing energy costs and creating jobs throughout the country. Whether Canadians are wearing a better parka to keep ourselves warm in the winter or installing a heat pump to reduce our energy bills, Canadians understand that staying warm should not mean wasting energy. Canadians also keep more money in their pocket.

I am thrilled that budget 2026 renews the green industrial facilities and manufacturing program, which, to my knowledge, is now called SHIFT, the strategic high-efficiency industrial facilities transition program. This $400-million investment will help optimize energy efficiency for Canadian industrial and manufacturing facilities in a way that will help us remain competitive while also lowering carbon emissions. As a strong advocate of energy efficiency measures, I am also deeply excited for the renewal of DRE, or the deep retrofit accelerator initiative.

Let us discuss transportation as well. We know that nearly one-fifth of Canada's greenhouse gas emissions come from the vehicles on our roads. Do members know that nearly 25% of global car sales this year will be electric vehicles? That is right. Everyone looks really impressed. Globally, one in four vehicles sold will be electric, and by 2030, 40% of new car sales will be EVs. The opposition is very excited about this change. Canada is huge, and we need infrastructure to change our cars. We need larger charging networks to connect Canadians, including rural communities. This is why I am electrified that budget 2026 supports the installation of 55,000 new EV chargers. That is about $600 million invested over five years to renew the zero-emission vehicle infrastructure program. This investment would mean 55,000 new EV chargers across Canada, with 9,000 in Quebec, 23,000 in Ontario, 17,000 in B.C. and many in Alberta and elsewhere.

As I wrap up, I would like to highlight a few other measures. The first one is on sustainable finance. I would like to thank the leadership of the member for Whitby as we continue to develop a new sustainable bond framework for government issuance using made-in-Canada sustainable investment guidelines. The second is on marine conservation. It is worth highlighting the investment of $282 million over 11 years for the creation of two new national marine conservation areas, as well as support for three more in the north. Canada has set ambitious targets of 30% conservation of its land and oceans by 2030, and this will help us get there.

If I may, I would also like to quickly mention that budget 2026 supports our national parks and historic sites. I would like to mention quickly the support for the Terry Fox Humanitarian Award, which does excellent work. In passing, my friend Ryan Keeping, who ran across Canada a few years ago, and his father, Scott Keeping, from Halifax are very big fans of Terry Fox. There is also the Canada groceries and essentials benefit program, which benefits all of us across our ridings.
Third, support for the Francophonie summit is also crucial. That is important to us.
In closing, budget 2026 is one that will help all Canadians, that is good for nature and the environment and that helps mitigate climate change.

Mr. Speaker, I note that the hon. member is a climate change champion and that he talked a lot about the clean energy investments his government is making. I want to ask about the productivity mega tax deduction. It is estimated that this tax deduction will provide a $2-billion annual tax break to Canada's oil and gas sector. We are certainly excited about that in Alberta.
I wonder if the member could tell us how excited he is that his government is providing a $2-billion tax break to Canada's oil and gas sector.

Mr. Speaker, I think you are excited about the budget from yesterday. I am very enthused about yesterday's budget. As I outlined, we had a lot of measures in there. I can sense your excitement. I know you are going to applaud the excitement for yesterday's budget. You are looking forward to going back to your riding, talking about the electricity funding and probably even the EV chargers that might be installed in some of your communities—

The member is now speaking directly to the member who just offered him a question. I remind the member to speak directly through the Speaker. I will let the member finish very briefly and then continue with questions and comments.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I think the member will appreciate the positive impact this will have on all communities.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather unbelievable that the government is sending out its green warriors this morning to try to make this budget seem green, when it is not green at all. What we are seeing this morning is greenwashing, and it is shameful to see the government members trying to make us believe that this is a green budget.

I would like the member for Honoré-Mercier to answer me in French, because he mentioned the importance of the francophonie, but he only spoke French for about 20 seconds of his 10-minute speech. That is really something else.

Let us talk about the environment. This budget includes billions of dollars in subsidies for fossil fuels. That money will be used to produce oil. It earmarks $43 billion for an oil sands pipeline. It includes funding to produce gas via hydraulic fracturing, which is banned in Quebec.

Is the member for Honoré-Mercier comfortable with the government's decision to continue with oil and gas subsidies? Is he comfortable with dismantling the climate change action plan, including industrial carbon pricing and the clean electricity strategy? Is he—
I have to give the member for Honoré-Mercier the opportunity to respond.

Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to answer questions from my colleague from Repentigny. I have known my colleague, who used to be with Greenpeace, for nearly a decade. I am used to his opposition to all governments.

I certainly hope that my colleague will be very excited that Quebec is getting 9,000 EV charging stations and that we are going to work in Churchill Falls to increase clean electricity generation. The Canadian Climate Institute supports our budget. Clean Energy Canada supports our budget. The Pembina Institute and the Transition Accelerator also support our budget. The list goes on and on.
I work very hard on the Standing Committee on Environment and Sustainable Development with my colleague, and I very much look forward to him standing up and supporting our budget.

Mr. Speaker, I am really glad that my colleague talked about transportation. We saw, in the budget, $1.2 billion for Marine Atlantic, for Atlantic Canadian ferry infrastructure, which is critical, as I know, from coastal communities. It is our marine highway and we support that.

When it comes to Vancouver Island and coastal communities, BC Ferries got nothing. In fact, we got a loan. We got an interest-bearing loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank instead. This inequity is not nation-building. In fact, we get $6 per capita for operating costs. Atlantic Canadians get $125.

When is the government going to stand up and invest in Vancouver Islanders and stop abandoning us? They elected two Liberal members. They have not done anything for us. They have abandoned Vancouver Islanders.

Mr. Speaker, the member opposite is a colleague and a great friend. I respect his advocacy for his riding enormously. I would like to highlight that in the budget there was over $280 million allocated for marine conservation. I am certain that the member will be very excited about our objective of increasing marine conservation from 15.5% up to 30%, which would benefit all Canadians, including the folks from Vancouver Island.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague supports energy efficiency and funding for energy-efficient projects.
Can he tell us a little more about how the budget will help us be more productive in that regard?
Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question.

As members know, a few weeks ago our government announced a $2-billion heat pump program, which will benefit one million Canadian households. Rebates of $10,000 will be awarded to lower-income Canadians. This will help reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 25 megatonnes. This is very positive for Canada.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will be splitting my time with the member for Calgary Crowfoot.

This budget fails to establish a credible fiscal anchor to reduce the debt and to balance the budget. The fiscal anchors of Liberal budgets of the past decade were ever-changing and never met. The Prime Minister has continued with that practice. The national debt is increasing, interest costs are starting to take off and there is no plan to balance the budget. Here are the consequences.

The Prime Minister risks losing credibility with financial markets because there is no credible fiscal anchor to reduce the debt and balance the budget. Canada's experience in the mid-1990s demonstrates how quickly things can change when investors lose confidence. Debt crises have their small beginnings when interest expense grows faster than nominal GDP, and that is exactly what is happening.

Interest expense on the debt is growing faster than nominal GDP, and interest on the national debt has now become the fastest-growing expense. Interest expense currently costs 11¢ of every tax dollar and is projected to rise to 14¢ in four short years. That is $85.5 billion a year, more than what the government spends on public health care. That is $8,000 a year for a typical family of four.

Canada has the smallest of the G7 currencies, and ours is not a reserve currency. Canada also has some of the highest levels of household indebtedness in the world and some of the highest income taxes in the G7, which means that households already struggling to pay the bills and struggling with affordability have little ability to pay more in tax. Canada has some of the highest levels of subnational debt in the world, for which the federal government is the backstop.

All this borrowing is also making life more unaffordable for individuals, families and companies. Massive increases in government debt compete with individuals, families and businesses for the money available to borrow from lenders. Lenders increase interest rates. The yields on the Government of Canada's five- and ten-year bonds have been rising in recent years. These are key benchmarks that determine the bank's cost of funds and interest rates for mortgages, lines of credit and car loans. These rising interest rates hit Canadian households particularly hard because of the high levels of household indebtedness in Canada, currently at $3.3 trillion.

Another consequence of rising debt and interest costs is that Canada is rapidly losing fiscal capacity to deal with a future major crisis. In the last 20 years, Canada has faced two major crises: the 2008 global financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic. In those cases, Canada's debt to GDP was roughly 30%, giving the government the fiscal firepower it needed to respond, and allowing the government to borrow upward of 5% to 15% of GDP in order to respond.

The Prime Minister has stated, in his recently released national security strategy, that we must be prepared for a major crisis. It states that Canada needs to prepare for all contingencies up to and including war and other worst-case scenarios, and has put economic security at the heart of that plan.

The next major crisis the Prime Minister says we must be prepared for requires fiscal capacity, just as was needed in 2008 and in 2020. The problem is that the debt is rising, and so are interest costs. They are reducing the capacity for the government to do that. The government's debt to GDP is currently 40% and climbing, and interest costs are starting to take off. This is leaving less and less fiscal capacity to deal with a future crisis the Prime Minister says we must be prepared for. While the government is not facing an immediate fiscal impasse, it has become complacent in not having credible fiscal anchors to reduce the deficit and the growth of the national debt.

All this spending in the budget also is not working. It is doubling down on what the previous Trudeau government did. In the Prime Minister's first budget, deficits over five years were double that of Mr. Trudeau's last budget. In the Prime Minister's second budget, spending has been obscured by pushing it off the budget onto the balance sheet by capitalizing borrowing. For all the talk of increased business investment, employment growth and economic activity, little is showing up in the numbers.

Food bank usage is at record highs, with some 2.35 million Canadians visiting a food bank each and every month, up 117% since 2019. Overall business capital formation has declined in five of the last six quarters and remains at the low levels of when Mr. Trudeau left office. Unemployment remains elevated, about 1% above pre-pandemic levels, because the economy is not generating enough jobs to push it down to roughly 5.5%. Productivity growth remains sluggish, if not non-existent, since the Bank of Canada declared a productivity emergency two and a half years ago. Economic growth remains stagnant, below 1% this year.

All these things, food bank usage, overall business capital formation, unemployment, productivity and economic growth, have changed little in the last 18 months under the government. That is because the government has failed to introduce the fundamental supply side reforms necessary to spur investment, create growth, and raise incomes and paycheques for Canadians, reforms such as an overhaul of Canada's competition policy to increase consumer choice and lower prices for struggling households; an overhaul of our taxes that the business community and experts have long called for in order to increase investment and incomes; an overhaul of our regulatory system, particularly for small- to medium-sized businesses; addressing interprovincial trade barriers; and so many other regulations that are strangling business and capital formation.

The last thing I would like to say is this. This budget is an affront to Parliament. It is a travesty of a document. First of all, it is incoherent and impossible to understand. There are several definitions of net debt in this document. Its accounting definitions, operating versus investment, are so vague that even financial experts are finding it impossible to understand exactly what is going on. Off-budget items have been so massively expanded by capitalizing them on the balance sheet that the deficit figure has become a completely useless figure, and the debt is growing at more than twice the pace of the deficit.

Here is the bigger travesty. The fact we had to wait this long to get the document is an outrage. The government made numerous announcements contained in the document months ago, outside the fiscal framework and outside Parliament. Parliamentarians should not have to learn about $36 billion in tax expenditures at some investment conference in downtown Toronto through the nightly news. This is the place where the Prime Minister should be telling Canadians how much the government plans to spend, how much it plans to tax, and how much it plans to borrow.

The government has spent most of the last year announcing spending and taxation at its own organized conferences and its own contrived photo ops outside Parliament. To add insult to injury, when it does finally have an opportunity to tell us exactly what is going on in the budget, it is obscured by all sorts of financial chicanery.

Finally, the head of government, for whom the budget document is supposed to be an aspirational and generational blueprint, is jetting off to yet another around-the-world tour, leaving us to pick through whatever gobbledygook this is. I have a message for the Prime Minister. This is not Goldman Sachs. This is not Brookfield. This is the Parliament of Canada, and democratic accountability in this place, particularly over the public purse and taxation, is sacrosanct. It is time to start showing up in Parliament and to start answering some questions.

Mr. Speaker, I believe our budget reflects a very responsible fiscal approach. In fact, the debt-to-GDP ratio is falling, and we achieved our fiscal targets a full year ahead of schedule. Moreover, in a period of trade uncertainty, it is important to invest and stimulate the Canadian economy, support our small and medium-sized enterprises and to make essential investments, such as in the fight against homelessness, for example.

With that in mind, the question I have for my colleague is this: Does he agree that we should make use of our fiscal flexibility? Canada is in a strong fiscal position to invest in Canadians' priorities, whether that means tackling homelessness, strengthening our national defence or supporting economic growth across the country.

Mr. Speaker, I think the problem is that, although we are not currently in a fiscal crisis, the government needs to prepare for future crises like the ones in 2008 or 2020, which forced the government to spend a great deal of money to support our fellow Canadians. The problem with the government's budget is that the national debt is 10% higher than it was in 2008 and 2020. The government is considerably reducing its ability to respond to a future crisis.
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague on his speech.

One thing that drew my attention as he spoke—probably because of my own academic training as an accountant—is everything he pointed out about deficit accounting, and what constitutes an expense, an investment or a debt. In the end, none of it makes any sense anymore. My colleague and I are not the only ones who cannot make heads nor tails of it. It would leave anyone with training in accounting, economics or finance completely in the dark. The system has become totally insane: Ottawa is using every trick in the book to hide the real status of the deficit. I agree with that.

I also greatly appreciated it when he mentioned that the only indication we have now about the actual state of things is when we see the debt increasing, because it has become so hard to hide. In any case, the right approach still eludes them.

My question for my colleague is this: What are the consequences of rising debt? The government keeps telling us that Canada has a AAA credit rating, but it seems to me that it has been repeating that line for a long time while deficits continue to grow. Can that really go on forever?
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. colleague is raising an important point about the debt.

The problem, first off, is that the government uses different definitions of net debt in the same document. The document opens with a net debt definition used by the International Monetary Fund. Later on, in the annexes, it uses a completely different definition of net debt. In fact, it does not even refer to it as net debt but simply as debt. The document is very confusing and very difficult to follow, because there are so many varying definitions for various items.

The second point I would make in response to my colleague's point is that the federal government is rapidly diminishing its capacity to respond to a future crisis that the Prime Minister says, in his national security statement, could be coming. In 2008 and 2020, the federal debt stood at roughly 30% of GDP, allowing the government to spend upwards of 15% of GDP to respond to that crisis. It now stands at 40% and is rising.

Mr. Speaker, last year in the House, the Prime Minister stated the government would deliver a declining level of debt, yet we have higher debt and a higher debt-to-GDP ratio. I wonder if my colleague could opine on the fact that the government has not delivered what the Prime Minister has promised.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague makes a very good point. The Prime Minister risks losing fiscal credibility with markets by following the pattern, frankly, of the previous Trudeau government in establishing ever-changing fiscal anchors and never meeting them.

We all saw this story play out in the mid-1990s. Markets can very quickly lose confidence in a government's ability to service its debt and to finance its operations. The bond markets have in recent years gone wobbly, as they have in recent months in the United States and in France. The government is not on a fiscally prudent track. The irony is that Mr. Trudeau's last budget was far more fiscally conservative, with deficits half of those of the current Prime Minister's budgets.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to speak about the budget, but before I get into the details of the budget, it is important to put it in the context of the government and its legacy since 2015. In 2015, when the Liberals were first elected, they inherited a balanced budget with a $2-billion surplus. We had an economy wherein housing was affordable, where a normal family with proper jobs or a person with a proper job could save their money and buy a house, across Canada. We had a country that had a middle class described by the very liberal New York Times as the world's most prosperous middle class.

There were pipelines approved. The northern gateway pipeline to the Pacific coast on the shortest route to Asian export markets was approved. The Keystone XL pipeline was approved. The Trans Mountain expansion was on the horizon with a private sector proponent. The energy east pipeline was on the horizon, to be proposed by TransCanada.

The Liberals blew it all. They immediately broke the promise they had made in the 2015 election to run only two years of modest deficits that would permit the budget to balance itself. They cancelled the northern gateway pipeline. They passed Bill C-48 to make sure it could never come back. They failed to champion Keystone XL. They chased the TransCanada pipeline out of Canada. The company changed its name to TC Energy and focused its investment activity in Mexico and the United States. They chased Kinder Morgan out of Canada and built the TMX at an extraordinary cost to the Canadian taxpayers.
This is the legacy of the government: broken promises and expenditures.

Minister Morneau repeatedly broke every fiscal promise. He declared this fiscal anchor of a declining debt-to-GDP ratio, as opposed to his election promise of a balanced budget, and then the Liberals blew through that promise and broke it repeatedly. His successor, Chrystia Freeland, in 2022 said that a declining debt-to-GDP ratio was “our fiscal anchor” and “a line we shall not cross” and that it could not be breached, in order to sustain their fiscal credibility.

Two years after that, the promise was broken again. She resigned rather than table a budget with a $30-billion deficit. We were here when an unsigned budget was just dropped on the table without a speech. It was extraordinary. That was just two years ago. Following the resignation of Prime Minister Trudeau, the current Prime Minister promised in the election that elected his government that there would be a declining debt to GDP. The Liberals broke that promise immediately. The PBO, as recently as just this month, has said debt is the fastest-growing expense of the federal government, and that brings us to the budget, which we had yesterday.

Before the budget, Conservatives had three asks. We asked for immediate relief for Canadian consumers who are unable to afford the high cost of living. We asked for the extension and removal of all taxes on fuel through to the spring, not just the excise tax but the whole range of federal impositions on the cost of fuel that make life unaffordable for Canadians.

We asked the government to stop its wasteful spending, and the Liberals delivered a budget that contains 150 billion dollars' worth of new spending. It is very difficult to follow the threads of their spending, as my colleague said before me, in this 500-page budget of confusing definitions and charts. We called upon the Liberals to rein in the spending so that interest does not end up choking out all other spending opportunities.
Our third ask was that they return to their anchor, or at least their stated anchor, of declining debt to GDP.

The anchors that have been cut loose and dropped to the bottom of the ocean by the government are astounding. There has never been a fiscal anchor that has held the government. The PBO said as much. The PBO's report said there is no evidence that the stated fiscal anchors put any meaningful restraint on the government's spending. Like a sailor, the Liberals buy an anchor. They do not tie it to the boat. They drop it overboard and realize that the boat is not being held. They go back to the chandler and buy another anchor, and everybody on the dock laughs at them.

We ask that the government finally hold itself to a meaningful fiscal anchor. A declining debt-to-GDP ratio is an anchor. It is something, at least. However, for a government that began its tenure with a balanced budget, a true fiscal anchor, I would suggest, would leave the government with the ability to cope with international crises and national emergencies, which happen much more often than people think. It is quite reasonable to expect that once every 10 years or so, there will be a catastrophic global event that will require massive support from the government. That is why it should be balancing the budget in the meantime. In a time of a growing world economy, the government should be balancing its budget and leaving fiscal capacity to run deficits in times of national emergency, not simply as a matter of course.

The government has added $750 billion to the national debt since members were elected in 2015. This budget proposes to add another $765 billion through to 2031. The Liberals have already given themselves extraordinary self-congratulations in their projection, claiming they will move up, by one year, the time at which they balance their so-called operating budget. What an utterly meaningless measurement of fiscal prudence that anchor is. It is rooted in accounting trickery wherein they can randomly choose how to classify their expenses in order to reduce whatever their so-called operating number would be and claim they have balanced it. Even the whole approach of meeting a fiscal anchor by something that is going to happen in the future is very typical of the government. It is always in the future, someday in some future year, going to deliver what it has promised today.

This budget is very disappointing. It does not address any of the three important asks that opposition parliamentarians raised with the government: making life affordable for Canadians, reining in its wasteful spending, and establishing a somewhat serious fiscal anchor and to actually be held by that anchor. Therefore, this budget is a disappointment. It is, as the member for Wellington—Halton Hills North said earlier, an affront to Parliament that the government would table a budget that adds extraordinary amounts of debt that is non-budgetary.

It is 500 pages long and very difficult to follow. The debt is accelerating faster than the deficits because of the way the government is accounting for its spending. This budget will not help make life more affordable for Canadians, it does not restore any type of fiscal discipline, and it leaves Canada vulnerable to future crises by eroding Canada's fiscal capacity to deal with uncertainty in the future. We have been warning these Liberals for 11 years that their reckless spending will leave us where interest chokes out other spending priorities.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mark Gerretsen (Kingston and the Islands, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I always get a kick out of listening to Conservatives tell us that they are great at balancing a budget and that they left a balanced budget when they left in 2015. When we look at the last two Conservative governments, of Brian Mulroney and Stephen Harper, they introduced 19 budgets. How many of those did they balance? They balanced three. Does anyone know why? The first two came on the heels of Paul Martin's surpluses. When Paul Martin, the Liberal finance minister and prime minister, left government, he left Stephen Harper with a surplus that allowed him to balance two budgets. Then he ran deficits for the rest.

How did Stephen Harper balance that one in 2015 that the member referenced at the beginning of his speech? He balanced it by selling off shares of GM at bargain prices. He balanced it by slashing veterans services and, for the first time in recorded history, had our defence at less than 1% of our GDP. Please, can the member tell me—
I have to interrupt to give the member for Calgary Crowfoot a chance to respond.
Mr. Speaker, I did not hear any contrition over all the broken promises the Liberals have made for 11 years.

If the member really wants to go back 40 years to Brian Mulroney, I might point out that when Brian Mulroney became prime minister of this country, Canada really, truly was in an absolute financial death spiral that had been left by Pierre Trudeau. I guess nine short years was not long enough to completely undo the fiscal vandalism of an even earlier Liberal government, so I will not take any lessons from him.
I may also remind the member that in 2008, it was his party that was ready to bring down the Harper government, in cahoots with the Bloc, over its refusal to spend even more and run a bigger deficit.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to recognize a local business' significant milestone. On November 1, Forte Workplace Law marked its 10th anniversary in business. It has maintained a strong focus on the community while building a reputation that extends well beyond South Surrey.

The firm has consistently supported local organizations while giving back through volunteer work in the community. It has also been a leader in helping make workplaces safer. The firm created Not Your Average Law Job, a national program recognizing lawyers who have built rewarding careers in a field facing burnout. Forte also created StandUP Teams, a bystander training program designed to address workplace bullying and harassment.

Founded by Sara Forte, the firm has since grown to nearly 30 people and has received numerous awards for its work. I congratulate Sara and the entire workplace law team on reaching this important milestone and thank them for their contributions to our community.
Mr. Speaker, they are the masters of a looming disaster.
Job one for the Liberal government should have been saving Canadians money on fuel, food and homes. Instead, they added $765 billion in new debt.
The Liberals keep claiming Conservatives are talking down Canada. We are not. We are calling out a government whose out of control spending keeps Canadians down and dependent on the government.

After 11 years, the Liberals have one answer for every problem, and it is another program, another bureaucracy, another billion dollars. They drive up the cost of living then hand Canadians another government program. That is not compassion; it is dependency by design.

The Liberals measure success by more spending, more programs and more sign-ups. For the Liberals, programs are more important than people, spending money is more important than getting results and growing government is more important than Canadians standing on their own feet. Success should not be measured by how many Canadians are signing up for programs, but by how many Canadians get off them.
The Liberal culture of dependency is a dangerous way of thinking. As long as the Liberals keep governing this way, they will keep making life worse for the Canadians they are trying to help.
Mr. Speaker, what began in 1951 with the marching mothers movement and volunteers going door-to-door collecting dimes in support of finding a cure to polio lives on today as March of Dimes.

This past summer, I had the pleasure of visiting with the wonderful staff and volunteers at March of Dimes in my riding of Don Valley North, and I want to take this occasion to congratulate them as they mark 75 years of service.

I advise the House of this remarkable organization because, throughout its history, March of Dimes has helped countless Canadians with disabilities overcome barriers and achieve their full potential. I commend it for its continued dedication to building a more accessible and inclusive Canada for generations to come.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's story keeps changing in his role in awarding a $2.3-billion contract to Telesat. The Prime Minister is in a blatant conflict of interest because the CEO of Telesat is none other than one of his closest personal friends.

The Prime Minister initially claimed that he had not discussed the contract with anyone in government, but yesterday his story changed. Yesterday, he said he was not part of the decision, but refused to say if he was part of the discussion. If he was part of the discussion, then that is illegal, and if he really was not involved, why is it that the Prime Minister has failed to issue the public declaration of recusal required by law?
We have had enough of the obfuscation, enough of the weasel words. The Prime Minister needs to come clean on Telesat.
Mr. Speaker, as we enter another November, I rise to recognize the Movember movement for men's health.

Movember brings light to some of the darkest topics, such as suicide. Unfortunately, three out of every four suicides are men. As someone who has nearly lost several people I care about deeply to suicide attempts, this cause hits close to home.
Our government is advancing Canada's first federal men and boys' health and well-being strategy to better support men's physical and mental health.

Today, I would like to speak to the men out there. They may not realize it all the time, but there are always people they can turn to. The world needs them, and they are enough. They do not have to face their challenges alone. In a moment of distress, remember that they can dial 988 and find someone to help them through.
This Movember, let us make time for conversations. Even when uncomfortable, they can make all the difference.
Mr. Speaker, it is Veterans' Week, and I am reminded that the story of service and sacrifice continues to be written by every generation.

On October 25, I joined veterans and serving members of the Canadian Armed Forces at Calgary Cenotaph for the dedication of a new plaque honouring those who served in Afghanistan. For many Canadians, remembrance brings to mind the sacrifices made long ago, but after September 11, 2001, a new generation answered the call to service. More than 40,000 Canadians served in Afghanistan over more than a decade, defending freedom, protecting vulnerable communities and upholding Canada's commitment to the world.

As we gather on November 11, we remember all who served and all who fell, including Calgary's own Corporal Nathan Hornburg, who was killed in Afghanistan in 2007. While we remember those who made the ultimate sacrifice, we also pay tribute to the dedicated members of our Armed Forces, who continue to serve both at home and abroad. May their sacrifice never be forgotten, lest we forget.

Mr. Speaker, it is my tremendous honour to celebrate the Ottawa Aboriginal Coalition on their 25th anniversary. The Ottawa Aboriginal Coalition is an amazing partnership of eight organizations supporting the urban indigenous community in Ottawa. They came together in 2001 to tackle a number of issues facing the community, with a particular focus on health and homelessness.

Last night, we had a remarkable community gathering with members of the urban indigenous community from Ottawa and with the broader community coming together to celebrate the Ottawa Aboriginal Coalition. It is the elders and speakers that are part of the coalition, and learning from their wisdom, that make the whole experience so worthy.
I want to congratulate the Ottawa Aboriginal Coalition for the tremendous work they do and wish them all the best for the next 25, 50 and 100 years.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Tako Van Popta (Langley Township—Fraser Heights, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government had one job, to make life more affordable for Canadians. Instead, the costly credit card budget adds a staggering $765 billion in new debt over five years, the largest borrowing spree in Canadian history.

The Prime Minister may divide spending across three credit cards to make it look smaller, but Canadians know the truth. Borrowed money must be paid back. That means higher debt interest costs, higher taxes in the future and more pressure on family budgets today. Conservatives called for relief on fuel, food and housing costs, and for a serious effort to reduce wasteful spending. Instead, the government plans even more spending while breaking its promise to reduce debt. The budget is not a plan for prosperity. It is a plan for being mastered by debt, and Canadians will be left paying the bill.

Mr. Speaker, on September 7, 1926, the Brandon business community chose collaboration and mutual support over competition. They understood that they could achieve more together, so they created the Chambre de commerce de Saint-Gabriel-de-Brandon, which expanded its catchment area in 1987 and became the Chambre de commerce Brandon.

Leveraging everyone's expertise and experience for the benefit of all, the Chambre de commerce Brandon has been working to ensure the economic and social development of its business community and its residents for 100 years now. By working together in a spirit of co-operation and partnership, the members of the Chambre de commerce Brandon are ensuring a positive and prosperous future for their community.

I want to acknowledge their extraordinary contribution to our community and their commitment to fairness, integrity and inclusion. One hundred years of commitment to sustainable development is remarkable and deserves recognition.
Happy 100th anniversary and best wishes for continued success.

Mr. Speaker, mental health is an issue I care about deeply. Over half of Canadians aged 40 or more have confronted a mental health problem at some point. They could be our friends, neighbours or loved ones.

In the Plateau and Mile End, we are fortunate to have the Regroupement des organismes pour hommes de l'Île de Montréal, or ROHIM, the Centre d'apprentissage parallèle, the Suivi communautaire le fil and many other community organizations to turn to. Our federal government has just announced a historic investment in mental health and addictions.

As Movember begins, we are reminded that one in five Canadians has already had a problem with mental health. That is huge, and we know that men have trouble breaking the silence. The results of our consultation on men and boys' health shows that we need to do much more, which is why our government is making a historic investment in mental health and addictions. I would like all those struggling out there to know that they matter and we see them. They deserve care when they need it, and they deserve it without judgment.
Mr. Speaker, as Remembrance Day approaches, we honour the Chinese Canadians of Force 136. For decades, their story has remained largely untold.

During the Second World War, they volunteered for dangerous secret missions behind enemy lines in Asia. They risked their lives for Canada while facing discrimination and being denied the right to vote at home. They fought for freedom overseas and helped advance equality at home. This week, I attended the unveiling of Canada Post's stamp honouring their service. Their stories show why recognition matters.

My motion, Motion No. 32, would designate June 22 as national Chinese Canadian contributions day and June as Chinese Canadian contributions month. I urge all members to support this motion and honour those who helped build and defend Canada. Lest we forget.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to proudly celebrate National Philanthropy Day.

National Philanthropy Day is celebrated on November 15 by networks such as Philanthropic Foundations Canada, Environment Funders Canada, Association of Fundraising Professionals and Imagine Canada, as well as thousands of philanthropic foundations, community foundations, donor-advised funds, charitable organizations and non-profit organizations.

I spent a decade working in the philanthropic sector, and I can attest personally that philanthropy helps strengthen society because it contributes to important public policy developments and advances issues that Canadians believe in. Philanthropy makes Canada strong because it helps build vibrant communities and active civic participation by bringing people and communities together.

On National Philanthropy Day, I encourage all Canadians to open their hearts, discover their moment to give, and thank philanthropic stakeholders, who give creatively and generously in ways that serve the public good and make Canada thrive.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians expect their government to manage public finances responsibly. That means a credible fiscal anchor to bring debt under control, a path to a balanced budget and a full accounting of government borrowing. This costly credit card budget falls well short.

Federal debt continues to rise with no plan to balance the overall budget. Debt interest will cost Canadians more than $60 billion this year, more than health care and more than national defence. CPP contributions are there to support Canadians' retirement. They should never be used as permission for Ottawa to borrow more. The $765 billion more in debt piled on in this budget will ultimately drive up interest rates and taxes.
For people in Waterdown, Paris and Binbrook in my area, this costly credit card budget means higher mortgage payments and higher car payments, the very last thing they can afford.
Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to be able to represent the people of my riding, Nipissing—Timiskaming, during the tabling of our budget, “Masters of our Destiny”.

I would really like to thank all of the citizens and organizations in Nipissing—Timiskaming who participated in the budget process. They submitted briefs and participated in round tables. I want to say a very special thank you to the North Bay and District Chamber of Commerce, because it organized a special round table for small business. I really look forward to coming back to my riding and speaking about the productivity mega deduction that applies to small businesses.
In closing, I want to thank the people of Nipissing—Timiskaming. On behalf of the government of Canada, I thank them.
Now, we move on to action.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, our troubles seemed so far away, but now it looks as though they are here to stay. The costly credit card budget told us about the government's aspirations, but today's job numbers reveal the results.

The job numbers are the report card on the government's performance. Unemployment is up 6.7% and youth unemployment jumped to 13.7%. Canada lost over 50,000 private sector jobs in the last month alone. That is over 50,000 private sector jobs in one month. Perhaps the most troubling is that the percentage of unemployed people who are finding work continues to decline. Less than 20% of unemployed people found a job in the last month. Almost 30% of Canadians are living in a household that has difficulty meeting their financial needs.

The budget contained almost no measures on employment and no response to constructive, Conservative proposals on jobs and families, and now we are seeing more job losses. Yesterday, we got the rhetoric. Today, we got the results. How we long for yesterday.
Mr. Speaker, to build Canada strong, we need strong rural communities, and that requires modern, sustainable infrastructure tailored to the needs of local residents.
Earlier this year, we launched the build communities strong fund, which enables us to invest in essential community infrastructure across the country, including in Madawaska—Restigouche.

Recently, I had the distinct pleasure of announcing a $2-million investment in Républik Nature to modernize its visitor centre and purchase a new all-season chairlift. These improvements will help ensure safe and reliable winter operations while supporting the expansion of summer activities, such as mountain biking. The project will generate meaningful benefits for tourism, the economy and the community.

I would also like to recognize the leadership and dedication of the entire Républik Nature team, as well as its volunteers, whose efforts have made Mont Farlagne a key asset for the vitality and quality of life in the Madawaska region.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, interest costs on the national debt are skyrocketing. By 2030, they will chew up 14¢ of every tax dollar, which is $85.5 billion a year and $8,000 for a typical family of four. That is more than we will spend on public health care, and more than we will spend on a whole range of other social programs. It is the fastest-growing expense in the government's budget.
What is the government going to do if we face another major crisis like we faced in 2008 and 2020?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member mentioned “fastest-growing”. Canada has the fastest-growing economy in the G7, as of quarter two results, at 3.3%. That has given us $27.5 billion more in revenue, with a lower deficit than projected in the spring economic update.

I am happy to confirm for the member opposite that the Government of Canada is exceeding its fiscal guardrails. We are balancing the operating budget one year ahead of schedule and sticking to our deficit-to-GDP ratio declining path.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, in most projections, growth remains anemic, below 1% this year, which is essentially zero.

Over the past six months, the government has announced tens of billions of dollars in tax expenditures outside of this place, which we only got the details of yesterday in the budget, so I have a simple question. Will the government commit that in the next six months, it is not going to be making any more major tax expenditure or spending announcements outside of this place, and will instead respect Parliament and announce them here?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what we will commit to is growing the Canadian economy as fast as possible to achieve what we promised Canadians, which is to have the strongest, most resilient economy in the G7. How do we do that? We leverage the strong fundamentals and fiscal firepower this country has to invest in Canadians, to support them with affordability measures like a boost to the groceries and essentials benefit, to move forward with our electricity strategy, to end homelessness and to ensure that we have a growing, prosperous economy that creates good-paying jobs for the future.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister chose his words very carefully yesterday when asked whether he had discussed the $2.3 billion given to his long-time friend and fundraiser Dan Goldberg, CEO of Telesat. He said that he was not involved in the decision. That was not the question.

Section 9 of Canada's Conflict of Interest Act prohibits public office holders from using their position to influence others to advance their own private interests and those of relatives or friends. Let us try this again. Has the Prime Minister ever discussed Telesat with his ministers, any of his staff, or public servants, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the question was asked yesterday, and the answer was provided many times yesterday. Canada has world-leading rules and regulations when it comes to ethics, disclosure and compliance. All members on this side of the House take that very seriously. The answer yesterday, as the answer is today, was that we follow these rules and we take them very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, that is the exact same response the Liberals gave as the SNC-Lavalin and WE scandals were unfolding. It is what they said on the green slush fund scandal and Trudeau's trip to billionaire island. In every case, after they repeated it, the truth came out.

Let us hear it one more time. Who wants to hear it one more time? Did the Prime Minister have any discussion about Telesat with any ministers, any staff or any public servants during or after 2.3 billion in tax dollars was given to a near bankrupt company run by a well-connected Liberal insider and friend of the Prime Minister, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, for those who have just tuned in, on the Conservative side, we have just entered the conspiracy TV segment of the show, where conspiracies come left, right and centre. Some are right-wing focused; some are really right-wing focused.
Again, we follow the rules here. The minister spoke to this. The Prime Minister spoke to this. We will always follow the rules on this side of the House.
Mr. Speaker, here is what Gérald Fillion said on Téléjournal yesterday: “We are back to the time-honoured tradition of big-spending Liberal budgets.”
The budget adds a record $765 billion in new debt over five years. That is $44,000 per household. Meanwhile, families are struggling to afford groceries and young people cannot afford a home.
Will the Liberals finally listen to us and agree to our plan to save Canadians money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we chose to make major investments in our economy. We made that choice because the time to invest is now. We are facing an existential threat to our economy now. Our neighbour is determined to completely disrupt our industrial sector.
We need to change our economy. To do that, the government must invest. We chose to invest. We also did not forget Canadians by proposing an important initiative to address homelessness.
Mr. Speaker, what would have actually been helpful would have been to cut taxes at the pump, because that affects everyone. That is a well-known fact.
The Conservatives proposed to eliminate all federal fuel taxes to save Canadians 20¢ a litre, or $1,200 per family. However, the Liberals chose instead to add $151 billion in additional spending.
My question is very simple: Why are the Liberals refusing to cut their spending and refusing to agree to our plan to save Canadians money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Caroline Desrochers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we, on this side of the House, are aware of the situation. We know that housing is one of the biggest expenses for families.

That is why, yesterday, we made historic investments in housing to continue the work that we began last year. We are recapitalizing Build Canada Homes to triple the construction of affordable housing. We are continuing to support programs under which tens of thousands of housing units are currently being built across Canada, including through the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, or CMHC.
The cornerstone of the budget is our investments to put an end to homelessness over the next 10 years.

Mr. Speaker, this budget got a very poor reception in Quebec. The president of Quebec's Treasury Board gave it a failing grade, and for good reason. Quebec simply asked that Ottawa not make cuts to health care. However, the budget confirms the federal government's intent to lower the health transfer escalator from 5% to 3% as of 2028. That means care that will not be provided and hospitals that will not be renovated.
Health care is a priority for Quebeckers. How can this government dare to table a budget with health care cuts?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rachel Bendayan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our budget includes historic investments to support mental health and fight addiction. In addition, at the municipal level, addressing homelessness is a priority for mayors. The new provincial government also sees addressing homelessness as a priority. At the federal level, we agree. We just announced a historic investment of $45 billion. We can and must work together.

Mr. Speaker, Quebec had two demands with respect to this budget: health care and the reimbursement of nearly $700 million owed to Quebec for welcoming asylum seekers, because we are the ones looking after them. The federal government has been dragging its feet on this debt to Quebec since 2024, when Quebec was taking in a disproportionate share of asylum seekers, without the federal government providing any assistance or ensuring fair distribution. As the saying goes, a debt paid is a friend kept. On this issue, however, the federal government has not been treating Quebec like a friend.
Why do the Liberals have money for everything except repaying their debts to Quebeckers?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Caroline Desrochers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as my colleague is well aware, we made historic investments in health care in the 2025 budget. We are continuing to do so in the 2026 budget, for example with a $2-billion program that will invest in mental health infrastructure and in tackling addiction, and with a new $5-million fund that will support projects that integrate social services, health and housing.
We are committed to this. We are going to end homelessness, and we will do so in partnership with the provinces and municipalities.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government does not have any money for Quebec's requests, including for health care, but it has plenty of money for Canadian propaganda. There is $300 million in the Liberal budget to plaster the maple leaf everywhere, $300 million to bring back Heritage Minutes and celebrate Canada's 160th anniversary. How nice is that? We will be able to watch the new Heritage Minutes on TV while we wait 12 hours in the emergency room.
It is absurd.
How can anyone be so out of touch with the priorities of Quebeckers?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rachel Bendayan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this budget makes massive investments in culture. That is good for Quebeckers.

It provides support for our artists on an unprecedented scale. It also provides support for our journalists. There is funding for the Francophonie summit and for expanding the presence of the French language across Canada
It is a good budget for Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance told this House that they had found $60 billion in savings in the expenditure review. His own deputy minister, though, stated that the review was merely an allocation exercise and that there were no actual savings. The costly credit card budget is showing an increase of billions in operating spending, adding to the already crushing debt load on Canadians.
Did the finance minister mislead the House, as his deputy and the budget show? If not, where is the $60 billion in savings?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are at a time when our sovereignty and economic security are being tested. What is the Government of Canada's response to that? It is to realize that our future is in our hands and that to build that future is our responsibility.

What we are doing is leveraging fiscal strength with fiscal responsibility to invest in the Canadian economy and to support Canadians with new affordability measures in this budget, like the groceries and essentials benefit and like making certain tax credits and extending them to encourage more investment and more growth. That is exactly what Canadians elected us to do.

Mr. Speaker, not wanting to be left out, the President of the Treasury Board, responsible for spending oversight, also stated that they had found $60 billion in savings. His deputy, though, contradicted him, calling it a “reallocation exercise” and stating there were no actual savings.

Here we have the two ministers most responsible for the public purse both claiming $60 billion in savings, yet the costly credit card budget shows an increase of billions in operating spending. Did both ministers mislead the House? If not, where is the $60 billion in savings?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, budget 2026 puts Canada's future in our hands. It is in our hands to build this country up. We have a growing economy, with 3.3% second quarter GDP growth. We found $27.5 billion less of a deficit, with a 9% increase in new business investment, and non-U.S. trade is up 56%.
We are putting Canada on track to enter an investment supercycle to see our economy go from $3.4 trillion to $4 trillion over the next number of years. That is progress. That is how we build Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in 2015, the Liberals promised two years of modest deficits that would lead the budget to balancing itself. Instead, they added $750 billion to the national debt through 11 years of credit card budgeting. Interest on national debt is now the fastest-growing government expense, threatening to choke out priorities like health care and national defence.
How can we trust the Liberals to get their spending under control when yesterday's budget adds another $765 billion to the national debt?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Corey Hogan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, managing debt is important, and so is intellectual honesty and context.

The reality is that our debt servicing is at 1.7% of GDP, comparable to the Harper years that they lionize, and well below the 6.5% in the nineties. We have the lowest net debt. We have the second-lowest deficit. We are using that fiscal capacity to grow our economy, including in our home city of Calgary, where we are seeing significant growth and significant investments, including tens of thousands of jobs and thousands of youth jobs.
There is much to be excited about. I hope they get on board.
The Speaker, for 11 years in a row, the government has tabled spending, borrowing and deficit projections that breached their previously promised targets, and the member wants to talk about honesty.
The projections in yesterday's budget confirm that they have broken last year's fiscal anchor of a declining deficit to GDP and the government's old fiscal anchor of a declining debt to GDP.
After 11 years of broken promises, how can Canadians trust the finance minister?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Corey Hogan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the deficit is down. Rents are down. Housing prices are down. Economic activity is up.
The plan is working. We welcome members to get on board.

Mr. Speaker, families in Richmond Centre—Marpole are cutting back on groceries and other essentials to make ends meet.
