They expect the government to show the same discipline, yet this costly credit card budget has another $62-billion deficit for this year and over $60 billion in debt interest, which is more than the Canada health transfer. A family of four will pay $6,000 just on Canada's interest payments.
This is a budget mastered by deficit. When will the Liberal government cut spending, reduce the deficit and give struggling families breathing room?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have great news this Friday. Budget 2026, announced yesterday, is leveraging our fiscal strength to support small businesses right across the country. With the productivity mega deduction, Canada is the most tax-competitive jurisdiction for new business investment in the world. From mines to mills to auto manufacturers and from bakers to dry cleaners, we are giving businesses the confidence, through a tax deduction, to invest in themselves today. With the Canada growth incentive, we are, more than ever, supporting successful entrepreneurs to reinvest—
The hon. member for Regina—Lewvan.

Mr. Speaker, let us try this again. There is no doubt that the AI minister, the Prime Minister and the Telesat CEO are good friends. They hang out together. They are in running clubs and book clubs. Their kids all go to the same rich private school, so there is a close relationship.
Why did the AI minister put Dan Goldberg of Telesat on his ethics screen but the Prime Minister did not?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what I will say is that when we look at Canada in terms of ethics and when we look at all the other rules and regulations as they pertain to ethics, Canada leads the way. As members of Parliament, all of us here follow them every single day, and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, after being here for a few years, I thought Justin Trudeau was going to have the most corrupt government ever in the history of the country, but the Prime Minister said, “Hold my beer. Watch this.” He is giving $2.3 billion to Telesat and to a close personal friend.
We all know the Prime Minister thinks he is better than the average Canadian, but why does the Prime Minister think he is above the law?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are about 15 minutes into question period and they have already jumped the shark three times. It is amazing.

Our country, again, has the most focused, stringent ethical rules of any nation in the world. We are focused on them every single day. The Prime Minister spoke about this on several occasions today, and the answer is that we follow the rules every single day. Why? It is the right thing for this country.
An hon. member: Oh, oh!

Order. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport is an able member. I know members are suggesting a lot of things he could say, but if they could just withhold them until after question period, they could suggest them to him at that point.
The hon. member for Repentigny.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government has delivered yet another budget that acts as though climate change did not exist. There is nothing in it to reverse the government's climate betrayal. The Liberals are not making amends for their historic rollbacks. On the contrary, they continue to subsidize oil and gas. They are weakening the clean electricity regulations. They want to generate more energy from gas and nuclear power. On top of that, they are weakening their industrial carbon pricing.
The only thing green in this budget is the picture on the cover. How can they table such a budget in 2026?
I would remind the member that members are not to hold up objects or hold props in their hands in the House, either during question period or during debate.
The hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rachel Bendayan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our nature strategy is the envy of the world. We are making historic investments in clean energy. I am thinking of our electricity strategy and the Churchill Falls project, which will be a game changer for Quebeckers and will capitalize on Hydro-Québec's expertise.
Our government is firmly and resolutely committed to growing the economy and protecting our environment.
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, Canada will arrive at the COP climate conference in Turkey with yet another budget that says the exact opposite of its lofty rhetoric.

In the meantime, on Thursday, the Auditor General said that Canada had quietly reneged on its promise to stop exporting thermal coal, the worst fossil fuel in the world. Canada had promised to stop exporting it by 2020. Since then, not only have exports continued, but they have also increased.
Does the government realize that it deserves to be tarred, feathered and driven out of COP?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Wade Grant (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am so honoured today that my son is on the Hill. He is 18 years old. This budget is about his generation, his future and what he is going to inherit.

We can build the economy while protecting the environment and protecting nature. His favourite place in the whole world is Haida Gwaii, on the coast of British Columbia. That is why we are investing $1.2 billion to protect our oceans and protect whales and in marine conservation, with $3.6 billion for the conservation of nature. We are also investing nearly $20 million to establish three new national marine conservation areas in the north.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's budget raises fundamental questions about the government's spending priorities. The government cannot claim fiscal responsibility while taxing the fuel rural Canadians rely on and committing billions to Alto high-speed rail. Families in Hastings—Lennox and Addington—Tyendinaga face the prospect of paying for a vanity project that could also take their land without any demonstrated business case. This is not responsible governance. It is a staggering disconnect from reality.
Will the government cancel Alto and put those billions toward the priorities of Canadian families?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, when it comes to high-speed rail, in particular this high-speed rail, it is a generational and transformational opportunity for Ontario and Quebec, boosting the GDP by up to $32 billion, with 50,000 jobs, and reducing our carbon footprint. The big thing, quite frankly, is that we are listening to Canadians. We are listening to Ontarians and Quebeckers with respect to high-speed rail. We have, we are and we will.

Mr. Speaker, the government keeps talking about its ambitions, but today's jobs report from Statistics Canada tells a very different story. Unemployment is up 6.7%, youth unemployment has jumped to 13.7% and 50,000 private sector jobs have vanished in just one month. Meanwhile, the government is projecting five more years of massive deficits, exceeding $50 billion annually, along with mounting debt servicing costs.
When will the government stop making promises and deliver a credible plan to create jobs and put Canadian finances back on a sustainable footing?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada has one of the lowest debt service costs in the world. We have a AAA credit rating, and long-term bond yields are rising less than other countries in the G7. Everyone in the world recognizes the strong fundamentals in the Canadian economy except the Conservative Party of Canada. It is the only one doubting Canadians and this country.
We will never apologize for investing in Canadians and putting our country on track for a prosperous future. That is what we were elected to do. When will they get on board?
Mr. Speaker, pretending one's grades are better than they are is not a way to improve one's performance.

The question was about jobs. The answer did not mention jobs. The budget barely mentioned jobs. We see the results today in the Statistics Canada jobs report. That report is not about aspirations; it is about results. Over 50,000 private sector jobs were lost in one month alone. Youth unemployment spiked. Unemployment overall spiked. Less than 20% of Canadians who were looking for a job found a job in the last month.
Canadians are struggling. Jobs are down. When will they actually fix the problem?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Stephanie McLean (Secretary of State (Seniors), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the budget that was tabled yesterday shows that we care about Canadians. It also shows that we are investing in the future of Canadian workers. Just yesterday, Canada's Building Trades Unions said:

Quote.QuotePara: Canada's Building Trades Unions (CBTU) welcomes the federal government's investments in infrastructure, housing, energy, and major projects in Budget 2026. These investments represent an important opportunity to build Canada's economy, strengthen energy security, and create good-paying, unionized jobs with lasting benefits for Canadian workers and their families.

Content.ParaText: Canadians believe in this budget. They should too.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have fittingly titled their new fiscal approach as though it is the next instalment of the Marvel universe. For over a decade now, Liberals have self-identified as heroes, unbound by the laws of physics or economics, and nothing is real. A former Liberal hero once made the fantastical claim that budgets would balance themselves. Now, in this fourth instalment, “masters of deception”, the Liberals' newest star, surrounded by the same old supporting cast, is using his cloaking superpower to render his gargantuan deficits invisible to the common eye.
Can anyone over there distinguish fantasy from reality anymore?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Corey Hogan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for that tour through the Conservative cinematic universe, but let us get back to the facts here. The reality is we have seen in our home province of Alberta an increase of 40,000 jobs since the start of the year. We are seeing debt servicing at low levels internationally. Our deficit is the second lowest in the G7, 2.5% compared to the U.S.'s 8.5%.
We are on track to meet the targets we said we were going to meet a year ahead of schedule, in fact.

Mr. Speaker, back in the real world, in 2015, Canada had a balanced budget and the richest middle class in the world. After a global economic meltdown, Canada's federal debt was $616 billion. Yesterday, we found out that after a decade of mismanagement, the Liberals' costly credit card budget would add more debt in the next five years than our country accumulated in 148 years. The Liberals have a predictable and increasingly tiresome response, an almost trance-like repetition of all the new things they are spending on in, entirely fuelled by massively out-of-control debt.
When will this unconstrained explosion of deficit spending end?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Sophie Chatel (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs and Associate Minister of National Defence, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, my colleague is speaking about heroes, but we are all wearing the poppy, and about the spending for our veterans. Here is what the budget would do. Veterans were always there for Canada, and we will be there for them. Our government is committed to ending veteran homelessness. That is what budget 2026 would do. It proposes $6.5 billion over 10 years to renew Reaching Home and the veteran homelessness program, supporting community-led initiatives to prevent and address homelessness. Those who serve our country deserve a safe place to—
The hon. member for Spadina—Harbourfront.

Mr. Speaker, Spadina—Harbourfront is home to one of the largest arts and culture communities in Canada. We know a thing or two about showcasing incredible Canadian talent and the artists who tell our stories. Budget 2026 includes much-needed investments to support professional artists and organizations experiencing financial pressures.
Could the parliamentary secretary tell us more about the measures included and how we are investing in Canada's cultural sovereignty?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for highlighting the important contributions that artists make to Canada's cultural identity. The proposed Canada creative credits in budget 2026 would help artists grow their creative businesses by providing tax relief on qualifying artistic income. Our government is also helping artists keep more of what they earn by expanding the expenses artists can deduct. Together, these measures will give our artists the tools and flexibility to grow their businesses and build lasting careers.

Mr. Speaker, we cannot become masters of our destiny by mortgaging our grandchildren's future. Canadians are trapped by Liberal debt. The projected deficit for the next five years is $288.7 billion, just for government operations, bringing the total to $1.593 trillion.
When will the Liberal government start thinking about returning to a balanced budget?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it has been said before that we should not be obsessed with balanced budgets. Now is not the time to get into that.

I, too, want to ensure that my grandchildren have a bright future. That is where we are going with two-thirds of our financial support measures. Two-thirds will go toward supporting the economy and increasing investment. Investing in our new economy is how we are going to ensure a bright future for our grandchildren.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are pushing today's problems down the road by cutting a cheque. They are offloading them onto my grandchildren. Maéva, Loïc, Béatrice, Delphine, Arthur, Mathilde, Clémence and Octave are calling on the Liberal government to take responsibility today so that they will not be crushed by debt tomorrow.
Will the Liberal government finally listen to the people who are going to foot the bill?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rachel Bendayan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I do not think my colleague has had the chance to read the budget in full. The figures we presented yesterday show that the deficit fell by 40% in 2025-26. In fact, we are balancing day-to-day spending a year ahead of schedule. Last year, we set two clear fiscal anchors: balance the operating budget and reduce the deficit-to-GDP ratio.
The 2026 budget that we presented yesterday meets both of these anchors and goes even further.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister claims his budget will make Canadians masters of their own destiny but with this massive debt binge, the only masters are global bankers and bondholders. The total deficit, projected at $150 billion, undermines our economy. Debt interest payments are now over $1 billion each week, and the fiscal guardrails are far in the rearview mirror. Canada lost over 50,000 private sector jobs just last month. Unemployment is up.
When will the Prime Minister finally master his credit card spending so that Canadians will not be mastered by his debt?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Corey Hogan (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I just want to remind my colleagues across the way that Stephen Harper ran deficits in seven of nine fiscal years.

In Alberta, we are seeing the plan we are putting in place go to work. We have 40,000 new jobs this year, 4,000 of which are youth jobs. We have the Pacific link pipeline under construction next year. We also have the pathways carbon capture project going. It is an exciting time to be a Canadian. It is an exciting time to be an Albertan. I really hope they get on board.
Mr. Speaker, if I mastered my own finances the same way the Prime Minister masters the budget, I would not qualify for a payday loan at Money Mart.

The Prime Minister told Canadians his deficit was only a measly $62 billion but when he includes his so-called investments, it reaches $150 billion. This kind of accounting trickery would not get someone a bank loan from the Prime Minister, but he keeps printing money and driving up inflation. Meanwhile, Canada lost 50,000 jobs just last month.
When will the Prime Minister finally get his costly credit card spending under control so that Canadians will not be mastered by his debt?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, why does it seem that Conservatives only seem to celebrate when they think Canada is failing? It is as if they are confirming what they really want every day in the House.

We are standing up and using the fiscal strength that Canada has to make the country stronger, to support Canadians with real affordability measures. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. We have seen the economy growing, and we are continuing to invest in jobs. In my region alone, 50,000 new jobs have been created by our government. There are billions of dollars of new investment. That is how we build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, let us talk a bit about that 50,000 figure. The member said that there is an aspiration in the budget to, at some point in the next five years, create 50,000 jobs. In today's job report, released today, we hear that 50,000 private sector jobs were already lost in the last month. That is not an aspiration. Those are real concrete numbers reported not by the finance minister but by Statistics Canada.

The government whip pretending that things are better than they are does not comfort Canadians at home who are struggling. He should stop pretending that things are better than they are and start fighting for people who matter.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is not aspirational when I mentioned 50,000 jobs. The new nuclear project at Darlington is 21,700 jobs in my region alone. The Pickering refurbishment project is another 30,000 jobs. Those are real jobs for real Canadians in my region. That is not aspirational. That is not hope. It is real action in the real economy, creating growth and good jobs for the future. That is exactly what we are about on this side.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised to make life affordable and get government spending under control. Instead, the Liberals gave Canadians a costly credit budget that should have been titled masters of debt. One in three Canadians is now skipping meals or eating less because they simply cannot afford groceries. While Canadians struggle to put food on the table, the Liberals continue to borrow billions and billions of dollars more, leaving taxpayers with the bill.
How much debt does the Prime Minister intend to pile onto Canadians before he admits that his approach of just throwing it on the tab is no substitute for reasonable fiscal policy?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, one of the first things that our government did when elected was to cut taxes for 22 million Canadians. We then entered into a comprehensive expenditure review and found $60 billion in savings over five years from government operations.

In the budget, we are leveraging that strength. We are enhancing the groceries and essentials benefit, offering hundreds more dollars per year to Canadian families. Twelve million Canadians are going to get more support this year as a result of the fiscal strength that our government has shown because our economy is growing. We will continue to invest in them.

Mr. Speaker, those programs clearly are not working, or they would not have put $100 million toward food banks that need more money to keep up with the pace of demand because of their policies. Families are already struggling with mortgages, groceries and gas. Half of Canadians say they have had to dip into their savings just to cover basic necessities, yet this year the federal government will spend $60 billion paying interest on the Liberals' debt.

That is more than we send to the provinces to deliver health care and nearly twice what families are provided through the Canada child benefit. With interest payments consuming more than 10% of the federal budget, when will the Prime Minister present a credible plan to get Liberal spending under control and reverse—
The hon. Secretary of State for Seniors.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Stephanie McLean (Secretary of State (Seniors), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this budget puts money in the pockets of Canadians, not tomorrow, but today. We are increasing the amount of the Canadian groceries and essentials benefit so that, with this one-time top-up, families of four will receive $2,570. That is real money that they can put toward groceries and can use to ensure that their children have a good start. However, we do not stop there. There is no consumer carbon tax. We have put a pause on the fuel excise tax. There is $10-a-day child care and school meals for up to 400,000 children. They laugh.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, Miranda Mamakwa died on September 8 due to complications from open-heart surgery because the Indigenous Services Canada non-insured health benefits program failed four times to organize her medical transportation to the south. She demanded justice in her final Facebook posts.
Nothing in this budget addresses the excessive transportation costs or lack of doctors for remote communities that need basic health care.

On top of housing, heating and grocery costs still being out of control, when will the Liberals realize that their aimless spending does nothing to address affordability and avoidable human costs forced on first nations?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Brendan Hanley (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, budget 2026 answers the call, with historic long-term investments that reflect the priorities of communities, from education and health care to essential infrastructure and supports.
Healthy people are the foundation of strong communities, so budget 2026 invests over $3 billion to support access to essential health care and strengthen public health in indigenous communities.
This is one of the many ways that we are supporting reconciliation and indigenous priorities in this budget.

Mr. Speaker, well, there is the real answer for Miranda's family regarding this budget: rhetoric through numbers to cover up their failure. Details show NHIB is frozen or less than next fiscal, which means more status quo and failure.

It gets worse. The Prime Minister promised to end homelessness in 10 years in this costly credit card budget, but the real number it does not tell us is that when we divide its allocation for housing over 600-plus first nations, it results in three houses per year for each first nation.
Have these Liberals actually convinced themselves that three houses per year will end homelessness on first nations?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Brendan Hanley (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that the member, who I work with on committee, brings up the question of housing. With budget 2026, we are committing $32 billion over the next 10 years for housing and infrastructure so that first nations communities have the stability they need today to build the stronger communities of tomorrow. This single commitment represents 60% more than all federal funding invested in first nations infrastructure since 2015. This is part of our government's plan to give first nations communities the certainty to think big and the stability to build for future generations.

Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege of representing the riding of Mont-Saint-Bruno—L'Acadie in the House. What makes me proud is seeing people from all over coming together to celebrate their identity and the richness of our francophone communities. Through festivals and stories, our artists and creators help to strengthen our feeling of belonging.
Can the government explain today how the budget will support our francophone communities and those who bring our culture to life?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Madeleine Chenette (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages and to the Secretary of State (Sport), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question and for the work that he does on environmental issues. Budget 2026 makes unprecedented investments in culture so that we can celebrate and protect what makes us Canadian. The budget includes investments in infrastructure and investments for our creators, artists, cultural institutions, media and journalists. I also want to point out that $339 million has been earmarked for the 2028 Francophonie summit.
Let us celebrate our francophone communities. Let us show pride in our culture both at home and abroad.

Mr. Speaker, nearly one in five young people in Windsor-Essex who wants to work cannot find a job. That is thousands of youth being denied the opportunity to get ahead, buy a home and build a future for themselves. After 10 years of the Liberal government, youth unemployment in Windsor-Essex is higher than the national average of 13.7%. Young people are paying the price for a decade of failed Liberal budgets.
Why does this Liberal budget have nothing for the youth in Windsor-Essex?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Peter Fragiskatos (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the general uncertainty that has been prompted by the tariffs levied against Canada in such an unjustified way has created uncertainty in business. We know that the Conservatives almost always fail to mention this, but it is a key point, and it is a key point relating to the youth unemployment rate.

The productivity mega deduction has been mentioned here at length today. It should be. It creates the most competitive tax jurisdiction in the industrialized world. That means investment. That means jobs. That means jobs for young people. Let us work together to continue to make this happen.

Mr. Speaker, when the power goes out, when forest fires burn wild and the highways close, people in my riding tune in to their radio stations such as Moose FM and Le Loup. When rural Canadians travel to work, they listen to their radio. However, the government spends only 3% of its advertising budget on local Canadian radio.
Without spending an extra dime, will the government give local radio its fair share of federal advertising?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Madeleine Chenette (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages and to the Secretary of State (Sport), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there is no question that our media are important and that they need to be protected and properly funded. That is what our budget is doing, once again. We will support our local media and encourage them to produce fact-based news and data so that Canadians can better understand local realities.

Mr. Speaker, this is about priorities. I am not asking the government to spend more. I am asking it to make better use of money that is already spent. Rural communities depend on local radio stations for breaking news.
Will the minister commit to redirecting a greater share of existing advertising dollars to local radio?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Madeleine Chenette (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages and to the Secretary of State (Sport), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for that question because it is certainly important for our government, without a doubt, to invest in local radio stations and journalists. That is exactly what we did once again in budget 2026. We are here to support the media, because they are such a force when it comes to gathering data and disseminating fact-based local news. Journalism is an extremely powerful tool for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, violent crime in Toronto has reached historic lows, with homicides and shootings declining significantly over the past two years. In fact, across Canada, homicides decreased by 125 in 2025 compared to 2024, which is the largest year-over-year decline in nearly 40 years. While there is more work to do, these results matter.
Can the Minister of Public Safety update the House on the actions our government has taken to contribute to this decline?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gary Anandasangaree (Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for University—Rosedale for her hard work. I also want to thank the brave men and women who put themselves in harm's way to protect Canadians each and every day. Their hard work is delivering results.

Our government has moved quickly to implement one of the most ambitious public safety agendas in a generation, with measures to combat organized crime, gun violence, cybercrime, auto theft and home invasions. We will not stop there. We will continue to give law enforcement the tools necessary to do its job more effectively.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government's new mastered-by-debt budget will make life even more unaffordable in Skeena—Bulkley Valley. There is no trade deal with the United States, $765 billion on the costly national credit card and more money for the Prime Minister's consulting friends. While the Prime Minister's friends benefit, last month nearly 30% of Canadians aged 15 and older lived in a household struggling to meet basic financial needs.
When will the Prime Minister stop piling on generational debt and start making life more affordable for Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rebecca Alty (Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our government understands the pressure Canadians are facing, and budget 2026 delivers concrete, affordable measures, including increasing the Canada groceries and essentials benefit by 50% in 2027, providing up to $1,290 for an individual and $2,570 for a family of four; investing $610.3 million in nutrition north to lower food costs in northern communities; and introducing the build Canada workers benefit to help workers keep more in their pocket.
Budget 2026 delivers affordability relief today while building a stronger—
The hon. member for Vancouver East.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister talks about building a stronger, more solvent Canada, but instead of protecting vital public services such as YVR and other major airports, he wants to sell them to private interests, putting affordability, safety and workers' rights at risk. Budget 2026 allocates $37.6 million to the privatization process. YVR has held the title of best airport in North America for 12 consecutive years.
Why is the Prime Minister letting corporate interests be the masters of our own destiny, and will he immediately reverse course and keep our public airports in public hands?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Mike Kelloway (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are focused on modernizing the airports. What that means is more investments in those airports. What that means is more service in those airports. That means more jobs in those airports. It also means looking at how things are done now and how they can be done differently in terms of sharing that investment with the regional networks to build up Canada from coast to coast to coast.
Mr. Speaker, what we are is award-winning.

Not only are the Liberals selling airports and our public assets, but Christmas came early for billionaires and corporate executives. Budget 2026 delivers $36 billion in mega deductions for corporations, but there is no mega deduction for everyday people. The temporary groceries benefit will quickly be swallowed up by rising food prices.

Instead of gifting corporations $36 billion in mega deductions, will the Prime Minister redirect those resources to build a network of public grocery stores to introduce competition and bring down prices?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Caroline Desrochers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the colleague knows very well that we are here for real Canadians with real programs. We are investing in affordable homes. We have committed to ending homelessness in the next 10 years. We are putting $10 billion through Build Canada Homes to build transitional housing, $5 billion to support projects that bring together housing and social projects, $6.5 million to renew the Reaching Home program and $2 billion for a health infrastructure that will help Canadians with mental health and addiction problems. We are here for Canadians, real Canadians.

I wish to draw the attention of hon. members to the presence in the gallery of Her Excellency Beate Meinl-Reisinger, Federal Minister for European and International Affairs for the Republic of Austria.
Some hon. members: Hear, hear!

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mark Gerretsen (Kingston and the Islands, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions, and I believe that if you seek it, you will find unanimous consent to allow the member for South Surrey—White Rock to repeat his S. O. 31.
Is it agreed?
An hon. member: No.

Mr. Speaker, Standing Order 16(2) specifically indicates that we are not supposed to interrupt people when they are speaking. I know that it certainly does happen in the House. However, when the member for South Surrey—White Rock was giving his S. O. 31, the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan was extremely loud in an otherwise very quiet room, directing some very personal comments toward the member.

I understand that something may have happened in committee that upset the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan, but the reality of the situation is that we have established a precedent. I would strongly encourage my colleagues to reconsider, because they know that they have found themselves in that position from time to time, and they would hate to set a precedent of starting to routinely shut statements down if this happens.

Perhaps at the very least, the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan could stand up and apologize to the member for South Surrey—White Rock for his actions while the latter was giving his S. O. 31.
The member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan is rising.
I invite members, if they rise on this point of order, to perhaps refer to the Standing Orders or past precedents without engaging in debate.
The hon. member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, the last time the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries rose in the House, he said the following: “It is interesting that the Conservatives have a member from Alberta asking questions about—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I am going to stop things now. I have risen, so no member will be recognized, and nothing will be in Hansard.

I did say to refer to a standing order or a previous practice of the House. I did not want to engage in debate over what happened and who said what to whom. That is not the role of the Speaker, and I do not want to engage in debate that members are having.

The rule is that members should withhold commentary. There is only one member recognized at a time during Statements by Members under Standing Order 31, and during question period. It is not a power that members have given to me to recognize multiple members at the same time. I invite members to withhold their commentary as best they can during S. O. 31 statements and during question period as well.

As Speaker, as a chair occupant, I do not have unlimited power to make you all quiet down. I know you are passionate individuals. You have a lot to say when you want to. That was a good reminder from the chief government whip about Standing Order 16(2). It also says to not cross between the person speaking and the Speaker, which some members are wanting to do.
There are other members wishing to rise on the same point of order.
I am going to give the floor to the member for Berthier—Maskinongé, but I do not want to start another debate.
I recognize the whip of the Bloc Québécois.
Mr. Speaker, I rise as the whip.

When a member is giving an S. O. 31 statement, particularly a member of a political party that has a lot of members here, the member may have to start over if there is a technical issue. It is customary to allow that. I was surprised to hear noes.
I would ask if it is possible to reconsider the matter, because, next time, it might be one of my members, and their request might be denied because somebody said no once.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. There are frequently comments and heckles during member statements and question period. The question is, with respect to Standing Order 16(2), where is the line crossed?

I think the reasonable expectation would be that if something interrupted the ability of the member to actually get a recording, if the sound was so loud that the intervention could not be properly heard, then I would say that violates Standing Order 16(2). My understanding is that, in this particular case, that did not happen, and in fact, the recording is fine. We cannot hear the commentary of the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan.
As a result, I suggest that Standing Order 16(2) was not, in this case, violated and that there therefore is no need to redo the S. O. 31 statement.
I am going to do something first, but then I am going to invoke Standing Order 10, which as members know is my favourite standing order because it says no more debating with the Speaker.

I will hear from the chief government whip, then the member for Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan. I do want to allow the member for Saanich—Gulf Islands to rise. She has indicated that she wishes to raise a different point of order.
The chief government whip.
Mr. Speaker, I do want to thank my colleague in the riding to the north of mine, the member for Lanark—Frontenac, because he is absolutely correct.

I think I would agree with him that there should be an establishment of breaking in one's speech and not being able to talk. If the member reviews the video of the S. O. 31, which he can do, he will see that the member for South Surrey—White Rock actually stopped at one point, waited and then restarted. We can see that; the video is there.
I just want to thank my colleague for coming to our defence. We really appreciate that.

Mr. Speaker, I had raised the issue previously of the grossly unparliamentary anti-Alberta remarks of that member. When I had, the Speaker responded, which is a matter of past practice, as you know. The Speaker said at the time, “It would not be proper if somebody did that, but unfortunately, the Chair did not hear that.” He later said, “I do not know [what] it was. I will check the record.”

The Speaker acknowledged that remarks of that character were improper. The Speaker has yet to come back to the House to rule on the unparliamentary anti-Alberta comments of the member for South Surrey—White Rock. I think that member needs to address the way he speaks about people from my region. If comments like that were made about members from B.C., where he is from, members from Quebec or members from Ontario, I think the House would have no problem acknowledging that they were unparliamentary and the member would have to retract those comments.
The member needs to be accountable for the way he talks about Alberta.
As I mentioned before these two new statements were made, the Speaker has said he will take the comments that were made and come back to the House, if required.

On this particular issue, as I said, I will invoke Standing Order 10. The chief government whip made a good point and reminded all members of Standing Order 16(2), to not intervene during statements and just in general in the House when one member is recognized by the chair occupant. Perhaps in the lobbies, the whips can negotiate, if they wish, for another UC motion.
However, on this particular issue, I am invoking Standing Order 10, so the House can proceed to its prearranged business that the government has set before the House.
With that being now said, I know that the member of Saanich—Gulf Islands has a different point of order she wishes to raise.
Mr. Speaker, my point of order, unusually at the end of the question period, relates to something that happened yesterday in this place at approximately four o'clock.

I think it was the member for Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay who had the floor and was speaking when the House was disrupted, very much contrary to Standing Order 16(2), in a gross violation of decorum. It was probably an accident that the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance thought it was appropriate to enter the House waving the budget and essentially turning this place of parliamentary business into a Liberal rally. I was deeply offended. I have never seen anything like it.

I know the Speaker called for order at the time and did his best to remind people to take their seats, but a presentation of a budget, and I have been to many of them, is a moment when members are keen to hear from the Minister of Finance, not to have the budget paraded as a document with lots of cheering and whooping it up.
I just wanted to put it on the record. The event has now passed, but people can find lots of photos of it on The Globe and Mail's website.
I understand the hon. member for Barrie South—Innisfil is rising on this point of order.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. On this point of order, related to the same standing order, I know you were in the chair yesterday when this happened. I was in the House. The Prime Minister and the finance minister walked in, waving the budget around like we were in some sort of Roman Colosseum. Maybe sometimes it seems that way, but I will say that I believe, Mr. Speaker, if you look back at the tapes, you will see that the member who was speaking was disrupted at that point as she was talking about government business.

I believe her privileges to speak freely and not be disrupted in this place with respect to government business were breached yesterday. I would ask that the Speaker take it back, look at the tapes and look at the way they entered this place and disrupted the proceedings of the House.

I will go back and review the tape specifically as to what happened, and recollect my memory, and then take it back to the Speaker for the Speaker to determine whether he needs to return to the House with a ruling. That will lay the matter closed for now.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to table a petition initiated by a Vancouver high school student, Elize Nocente, and signed by over 1,500 people to shine a light on endometriosis. Up to two million girls, women and gender-diverse people in Canada are affected by this. The petitioners say Canada has no national action plan, no coordinated federal funding line and no standard clinical guidelines for the disease and that research is underfunded.

The diagnosis delay for endometriosis averages 11 to 12 years, and the petitioners say a mandatory endometriosis education program would help correct this. They call on the Government of Canada to, first, fund a national advisory board on endometriosis education that would develop evidence-based education and resources for use in secondary schools, increase public awareness and allow people to recognize signs of the disease early on and, second, to work with provinces and territories to support mandatory inclusion of endometriosis education in curricula.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government, of the amendment and of the amendment to the amendment.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Vancouver East.
Budget day is a big day for all Canadians. There is no question that our world has changed. We also know that Canada has the innovation, resources and talent to be stronger than it was before.

I spent much of yesterday combing through the budget for all of the details that I know will positively impact my riding of Spadina—Harbourfront. I am thrilled to rise today to add my voice in support of budget 2026. I believe strongly that it is a budget that invests in people and shapes Canada's future. Budgets can be aspirational, but this one is also practical, with real measures that support Canadians.
In a country where we are masters of our destiny, we must be able to live, work, and build our lives while being free to choose our own destiny.

Budget 2026 proposes to enhance the Canada groceries and essentials benefit, with an additional payment that will raise the support in 2026-27 to about $1,290 for a single person without children and $2,570 for a couple with two children. Not only would the Canada groceries and essentials benefit lift an additional 120,000 people out of poverty in 2027, but we would see a measurable impact on the lives of women and girls.

A job should allow Canadians to earn a decent living. Unfortunately, that is not always the case. That is why budget 2026 proposes to enhance the Canada workers benefit by introducing the build Canada workers benefit.

Nearly two million low-income workers would receive increased assistance, including 180,000 new recipients. For workers with the lowest earnings, this could mean up to $675 more per year, and even more for those eligible for the disability supplement. Taken together, the benefit would lift an estimated 240,000 people out of poverty.
Building a stronger economy also means supporting those who care for others.

We cannot speak about affordability measures without speaking about those who are experiencing homelessness in Toronto. This includes families and children who are struggling to find a safe place to call home. Organizations in my riding, such as West Neighbourhood House, The Neighbourhood Group, CAMH, Parkdale Queen West Community Health Centre, St. Felix Centre and Homes First have been on the front lines working hard to support our community members, and our government has been working on this issue since day one. We know and understand that everyone deserves access to safe and affordable housing.

In September, alongside the Accelerating Accessibility Coalition, I convened a round table on accessibility, community connection, health and multi-generational livability along Toronto's waterfront. The costs of homelessness extend far beyond street homelessness. Residents have told me how important it is that they can continue to live in their communities and not be pushed out to end up looking to shelters as alternatives. This underscores the importance of our launch of Build Canada Homes to increase housing supply and build more affordable homes.

Budget 2026 sets Canada on an ambitious path to end homelessness over the next decade. We are providing almost $30 billion to move people from homelessness into stable housing. Our housing plan would address the mental health and substance use challenges that are contributing to homelessness, instability and growing pressures on communities across Canada. Homelessness is a complex challenge that does not have a simple solution. It is a responsibility shared across multiple levels of government.

Our federal government is doing our part. This includes $32 billion over 10 years for first nations housing and infrastructure and the launch of a first nations on-reserve infrastructure program. This amounts to nearly $45 billion in new housing investments that will strengthen Canada's housing system, expand affordable and non-market housing and ensure that the housing market works better for everyone. We must build in all parts of Canada and ensure that those most vulnerable are not left behind.

Budget 2026 is also about building opportunities to showcase Canadian identity. Spadina—Harbourfront hosts one of the most vibrant arts and culture sectors in Canada. Downtown Toronto is a site for tourists, residents and all who enjoy the arts. We have performance spaces, galleries, festivals and cultural organizations such as TIFF, the Ed Mirvish Theatre, Harbourfront Centre and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra, just to name a few, that bring the magic of creativity and innovation into our lives.

It is no secret that I love the arts and that the collective of makers, designers and creatives I have met over the course of the last year has made an impact on the way I do my work here as a member of Parliament.

I know the vital role arts and culture plays in our economy, our community and our national identity. Their contribution speaks for itself. Canada's arts and culture sector contributed $65 billion in direct GDP in 2024, supports 13 jobs for every $1 million in economic output and generates an estimated $17 billion in federal and provincial tax revenue. In fact, the sector has grown faster than many traditional industries in recent years and supports hundreds of thousands of great jobs across this country.

This is why budget 2026 proposes to invest $4 billion for arts and culture to protect and celebrate what makes us Canadian. This includes our government's intention to establish a new Canada creative credit to support artists. Canadian artists will not pay tax on up to $45,000 of income derived from their creative work. I have already heard from stakeholders in my riding who immediately know the impact this will have on working artists and students who are looking to build their careers in the arts, but we have not stopped there. We are also strengthening Canadian film, media and journalism, CBC/Radio-Canada and our national cultural institutions.

We are also bringing back the Canada strong pass, giving Canadians the opportunity to fully explore their communities and the people and places that make them unique. Budget 2026 would renew the Canada strong pass for summer 2027, making it permanently free for young Canadians under 25 to visit our national museums year-round. Not only does this provide free admission to Parks Canada sites and participating museums and galleries, but also savings on Via Rail travel.

Spadina—Harbourfront is home to the iconic Union Station, and I know first-hand that the influx of visitors has enormously benefited small business owners in our neighbourhood. What an incredible opportunity for more children and young adults to engage more with the art, history and stories that define our country and connect with Canada's natural beauty through our national parks.

The businesses that live on the periphery of downtown tourism and of arts and culture also need opportunities to thrive. Over Thanksgiving, I hosted a small business round table and heard from a wide range of business owners and operators about the opportunities they also saw for themselves in Toronto. Business owners are community leaders. They are job creators, and they draw people into the vibrancy of our neighbourhoods. One operator described how quickly they were losing U.S. corporate bookings following tariff announcements. Others explained that uncertainty in planning for next year's costs was forcing them to scale back their plans today. These conversations made it clear how uncertainty can hold back investment, even when business owners see opportunities to grow.

In September 2026, our government announced the productivity mega deduction. Building on the productivity superdeduction introduced last year, this measure would allow businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of a broader range of capital assets, covering more than 65% of investment on a permanent basis. It would bring Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new business investments down by half. If a business is ready to invest, that means a lower after-tax cost of getting new equipment to expand or increase their operations.

A stronger Canada is a Canada where we are masters of our destiny, and that starts with giving Canadians the means to move forward, the freedom to make their own choices, and the ability to build their own future.

I believe deeply in a Canada where every person, no matter where they start, has a fair shot at a great life. I believe that a Canada where we invest in people, not cut them off, demonstrates to Canadians that we show up when they need us most. To achieve this for Canadians, we must strengthen our economy so that decisions made by other world leaders do not dictate the direction of our future. We must build a Canada that gives Canadians the tools and the means to be the masters of our own destiny and, as a country, to chart our own course.

I am proud to support this budget because I believe it would move us closer to that future. As our Prime Minister has said, “Nostalgia is not a strategy”. We cannot build Canada's future by waiting for the past to return. We have to invest in the people who will build what is coming next.
