SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government, of the amendment and of the amendment to the amendment.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, yesterday's budget included tax measures for artists. If someone is a Canadian artist, for example, they will not have to pay tax on their income up to $45,000. The member mentioned TIFF, the Toronto International Film Festival. I am a big fan myself.
Can the member for Spadina—Harbourfront outline other examples of how this tax measure would benefit the fine residents of her constituency?

Mr. Speaker, OCAD University, one of the important post-secondary institutions in my riding, is really thrilled about this particular measure to support the income of artists. We know there are affordability challenges, and we know that people getting started in the arts need a real shot at this. The investments overall, the $4 billion in arts and culture, are going to make a significant difference for fighting for arts and culture in our country.

Mr. Speaker, the presented budget would bring lots of debt to Canadian households, which is something that would be unbearable. It is already unbearable and will become even worse in a few years. Somebody has to pay this debt, and that somebody is our future generations.
Is the hon. member not worried about how much debt Canadians will have to take on in the next years just because of the way the government has been handling the books?

Mr. Speaker, we are living through a time of real global crisis, and that means our government needs to respond with supports and the resourcing to make sure people do not fall behind. The systemic investments that will improve our country need to happen now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to know whether my colleague opposite is as disappointed as I am by her government's decision not to maintain the health transfer escalator at a level that reflects the actual increase in health care costs. It has to be said: There was just one high-priority request from the Government of Quebec, and it was also shared by other provinces, namely an adequate health transfer escalator. Once again, the government has found a way to run up an incredible deficit. It had money for all sorts of things, but not for health. Why is that?

Mr. Speaker, I want to remind my colleague that, in sections 91 and 92, the primary driver of responsibility for health care is the provinces. While we know how important it is to make investments in health care and be a partner to our provinces, we cannot shoulder all of it. We are continuing to make very important investments in mental health, in supports. We are making sure we are serving all Canadians, but we want to stay in our lane and focus on the things we are responsible for at the federal government level.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague just made reference to the health care system. Obviously, I assume we have all heard many stories of families or loved ones facing challenges going through our health care system. I am curious what the member thinks about the fact that the totality of all of the money we send to provinces to deliver that health care system has been now dwarfed by the interest on the debt the Liberal government has accrued, and this will be getting worse year over year.
Why is it better to send money to bankers and bondholders than to help people in our health care system?

Mr. Speaker, one of the things we are doing extraordinarily well in this budget is making significant generational investments in indigenous reconciliation with nearly $50 billion in investment in new measures that allow indigenous communities to get to reconciliation. This is a way of supporting Canadians who need support in these times.
Mr. Speaker, there were high expectations for this budget, but unfortunately, it misses the mark. This budget benefits the wealthy at the expense of the working class in this country.

The Prime Minister talks about the masters of our destiny, but who are they? They are the billionaires and corporate executives he invited to his exclusive investment summit. When we look at this budget, it is clear whose interests come first. Christmas came early for CEOs, foreign investors and arms dealers in this budget. The single biggest item Santa Claus is bringing is a $36-billion mega deduction, over five years for big corporations, more than all the affordability measures that he purports to champion for everyday people. Where is the mega deduction on grocery bills for everyday Canadians? Where is it on their rent? Where is it on their cellphone bill?

The government talks a lot about affordability, but this budget does very little to bring down the cost of living for everyday people. Instead, it doubles down on the familiar promise that if we give enough money to the biggest corporations and investors, somehow everyone will benefit.

Canadians have heard that promise before. It has not solved the affordability crisis. The government will say that it is spending $4 billion on a one-time increase to the Canada groceries and essentials benefit, which is a fraction compared to the $36-billion mega deduction for corporations. For a single person, that amounts to $267 a year, roughly $20 a month. That money will quickly be swallowed up by rising food prices. It is a temporary measure that does nothing to address the underlying causes of the grocery crisis.

One in three Canadians is skipping meals. Food bank use is at a record high. The government has no plan to confront the market concentration and pricing power of Canada's major grocery chains. The NDP has proposed real solutions: a network of public grocery stores to introduce competition and bring down prices, and a ban on surveillance pricing so corporations cannot use people's personal data to charge them more. We need to tackle the problems at their source, not simply give people a temporary payment while the big grocery chains continue to profit.

On housing, the government has announced that it will end homelessness and expand non-market housing. I love that. On the face of it, it sounds like good news. To end homelessness, Canada needs deeply affordable non-market housing. Experts say that Canada needs at least 200,000 net new non-market homes per year for three decades. Budget 2026 is proposing to deliver 24,000 non-market homes for 10 years.

That is just on capital investment. On supportive and operating costs, at least $5.7 billion per year is needed. This plan is entirely dependent on the provinces and territories, which are expected to pay for ongoing operations and wraparound services, including health care and mental health and addiction supports.

A building without the necessary operating funding for deep core and support services is not a solution to homelessness. The housing minister would know this better than anyone else. He promised to end homelessness in Vancouver when he was the mayor of Vancouver. Instead of delivering on that promise, homelessness grew under his watch. He blamed the federal and provincial governments for failing to provide the funding at the scale necessary.

Since the federal government is not stepping up with operating costs under budget 2026, my question is this: Has the Minister of Housing secured the operating and wraparound funding from the provinces and territories to deliver on the Prime Minister's promise to end homelessness? If not, this will become just another broken promise.

On another metric, the government admitted that Canada failed to build enough non-profit housing. We need to build a million non-profit homes to make a dent in the housing crisis, yet the commitments under budget 2026 are not even one-quarter of that ambition, nowhere near the postwar housing program the Prime Minister promised during the election campaign.
I will say this. The budget is not all bad news. The renewal funding for Reaching Home and the Canada housing benefit is good news and something I strongly advocated for.

Let me turn to another issue. While the government finds billions for corporate tax breaks and military spending, the cupboards are bare when it comes to essential public services. There is no new investment in child care. There is no increase to the Canada health transfer. The NDP called for an escalator of at least 6% to help the provinces and territories meet growing health care needs. Pharmacare is not even mentioned once in this 511-page budget. People cannot find family doctors. They wait months for treatment. They pay out of pocket for medication.

Rather than strengthen the public services Canadians depend on, the government is allowing them to erode. Meanwhile, one in five federal dollars is going to military spending, rising to one in four by 2030. Canadians deserve to know why there is so much money for weapons and war, but so little for the services that help people live with dignity.

This budget also lays out the groundwork for the privatization of Canada's airports, with $37.6 million allocated to prepare for that process and the expected legislation. Canadians should be very concerned. YVR is one of the best airports in the world. Privatization can mean higher costs for travellers, pressure to cut jobs and working conditions, and public assets being turned into opportunities for private investors to extract profits. Our airports are essential infrastructure. The Prime Minister does not have the mandate to privatize them. They should serve the public interest, not become another vehicle for private wealth accumulation.

There is another glaring omission in this budget. There is nothing meaningful to ask the wealthiest Canadians and largest corporations to pay their fair share. Canada's 40 billionaires increased their collective wealth by $95 billion in 2024-25, a 20% increase, yet this budget offers no new wealth tax and no serious new revenue measures targeting those with the greatest ability to pay.

The NDP has called for a wealth tax on very rich Canadians, and that could generate up to $40 billion a year. Think about that. Instead of giving corporations a $36-billion annual mega deduction, we could be asking those who have accumulated extraordinary wealth to contribute more to the country that helped make that wealth possible. Public money should come with public interest conditions, good union jobs, Canadian investment, accountability and a fair return to Canadians. We should be investing in productive infrastructure, in public services and in things that make life better, not simply hoping that corporate tax breaks will trickle down.

On climate, the government's priorities are equally difficult to reconcile. There is approximately $4 billion over 10 years for clean electricity, compared to $55 billion in public financing and investment for a pipeline. Bill C-39 attacks the environment and indigenous and labour rights. We cannot claim to be building a clean energy future while continuing to put enormous public resources behind fossil fuel infrastructure. The Prime Minister is driving up emissions, the same person who used to be the UN special envoy for climate and finance. Canada needs investment in renewable energy, a modern electricity grid and a just transition that puts workers and communities at the centre.

The Prime Minister tells us that the masters of our destiny are those who will build Canada's future, but the masters of our destinies in this budget are not Canadians and their families. They are the CEOs, billionaire and investors invited to the Prime Minister's investment summit. Brookfield, BlackRock and the big banks will be happy, but Canadians deserve a budget that puts the affordability crisis for families first.

Lastly, let me turn to immigration for a brief moment. The government has committed to transitioning 100,000 temporary residents to permanent status, and it is about time. That transition is welcome, and I hope it is only the first step in regularization.

I also want to note that outside of the budget, there is a one-time addition to the levels plan of 100,000 PR spots, which will include humanitarian applications for Hong Kong lifeboat people and Ukrainians. I have stood with them to fight for this from day one, and this announcement shows what happens when impacted communities and allies come together to demand fairness. That is justice. That is fairness.

Mr. Speaker, the budget provides financial support of nearly $600 million for electric vehicle chargers, with 55,000 new EV chargers across the country and 17,000 in B.C. I know the members for Portage—Lisgar and Vancouver Quadra are extremely excited about this new program. I wonder if the member for Vancouver East is also excited for this program and the impact it will have in her riding.

Mr. Speaker, I would be very excited, actually, if the Liberal government prioritized a climate strategy instead of building a pipeline, putting $55 billion into it, that will decimate the climate, do little to address the crisis we are faced with and exacerbate the situation we are faced with. Instead of putting $55 billion into a pipeline, we should redirect those resources to climate action, including EV vehicles and other environmental measures that are necessary for our climate.

Mr. Speaker, related to my hon. colleague's last question and her answer, I wonder if the member is aware of the value of the productivity mega tax deduction for Canada's oil and gas sector. Much of the revenue the government has projected to raise in the next few years relies on the success of our oil and gas sector.
I wonder if the member can tell us how excited she is about the productivity mega tax deduction benefits for the Canadian oil and gas sector.

Mr. Speaker, I just came back from COP17, which was a UN conference on biodiversity, and guess what. Canada is not making its targets. The 30 by 30 goals are not going to happen under the current situation, and that is not considering Bill C-39 and the ramming through of environmental strategies, environmental protections, indigenous rights and so on.

If we are going to talk about protecting the environment, I will ask the member and all members of the House, including those in the government, this question: Where is the Prime Minister who was the climate envoy at the UN and who once upon a time talked about the importance of finance and marrying the economy to the environment?
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my hon. colleague from Vancouver East. She raised many good points.

One thing I was surprised by was from earlier today. One of the Liberals who were speaking to the budget said that it was really committed to robust cost-benefit analysis. However, there is no cost-benefit analysis anywhere, neither robust nor otherwise, for the proposed and now approved Pacific link pipeline. The government is moving ahead with it as a major project of “national interest” with no cost-benefit analysis.
I wonder if my hon. colleague is as troubled by that as I am, since we are paying for it.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my good colleague for her advocacy, always, for the environment and the people.

She is exactly right. There is no cost-benefit analysis. The other thing that has been pointed out is that businesses are not required to do an impact assessment on the environment with their businesses. Less than 1% of businesses actually do that work. I asked the minister directly at COP17 whether the Liberal government will impose this regulatory requirement so that we know what the impacts are. Not only is the government not doing a cost-benefit analysis, but it is not making businesses do impact assessments, which is absolutely essential when the government wants to build a pipeline that will absolutely decimate our environment.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her excellent speech. I would like to know what she thinks about the fact that the government is claiming that it has an electrification strategy when it has actually only allocated $2.4 billion between now and 2030 for the clean electricity and clean technology investment tax credits. The government is weakening its own clean electricity regulations. It is going to cost the government $22.8 million to weaken a regulation that we have already paid to implement, all to please the gas companies and generate more electricity from natural gas.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my good colleague for his work and advocacy.

He is exactly spot on. The Prime Minister and the Liberal government will not hesitate one bit in dumping $55 billion into a pipeline that will decimate our environment. What we are seeing right now is the backsliding of a Liberal government on Canada's environmental strategy. That is clear as day. The investment that it put into climate initiatives is a drop in the bucket when we compare it to the big oil investments that the Prime Minister is all too eager to dump—
Resuming debate, the hon. member for Lévis—Lotbinière.
Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Calgary Centre.

When we look at the budget this Liberal government is presenting, we have to wonder what happened to all of its big promises. The government promised an ambitious budget. It talked about growth, productivity, streamlining and a new way of doing things. Rhetoric aside, once one has actually read the budget and looked at the numbers, what is left? Not much. This budget is all sizzle and no steak. The truth is that Canadians do not need big announcements. They need to be able to afford their groceries, mortgage, rent and bills at the end of the month. They want to know that their hard-earned money is being put to good use, but this budget is not very reassuring for them.

Let me start with public finances. The government is patting itself on the back for getting additional revenue, but we need to look at where a lot of that money is coming from. One of the reasons government revenues are going up is because prices are going up, because inflation is driving up nominal revenues and tax revenues. Although the government is taking in more money, Canadian families are paying more to fill their grocery carts. It is easy for the government to pat itself on the back for this additional revenue when it is Canadians who are the ones paying the inflation bill. The Liberal government seems to be forgetting one thing: When the price of gas, bread, meat or housing goes up, it is not good news for families. It means less money in their pockets. Inflation is the worst form of taxation, because it takes what little the middle class has left and makes the rich richer.

Despite this additional revenue, the Liberals continue to spend recklessly. Let us look at the numbers. The projected deficit for this year is $62.3 billion. In five years, in 2030-31, it will still be $52.9 billion, according to estimates. That is $288.7 billion in accumulated deficits over five years for government operations. That is a mountain of debt that we are leaving to our children and grandchildren, and that is not all. This year, the government will spend $60.2 billion on interest payments on the debt. In five years, that amount will have grown to $85.5 billion, meaning $25.3 billion more per year. That is more than all the revenue collected from the GST in Canada.

That is money none of us will never see again, unless we happen to be among the Prime Minister's banker buddies or other friends. Imagine what that money could do for our hospitals, schools, infrastructure and families. Unfortunately, it is going toward interest payments. We cannot build a country by working only to pay interest on the debt. It is all well and good for the government to talk about a balanced operating budget, but the overall budget is not balanced. The deficit is still there, year after year. It is a structural deficit. We will not become masters of our destiny by mortgaging our grandchildren's future. Canadians are trapped by Liberal debt.

Now let us talk about the cost of living. The Liberals are announcing a supplement to the Canada groceries and essentials benefit that will provide up to $339 for a single person and $679 for a family of four. It is all well and good to send a cheque, but does that lower the cost of the grocery basket? Does it lower food prices? The answer is no. A one-time cheque does not solve the problem. It helps some families for a while, but it does not make the cost of living go away. It does not address the root cause of the problem. Instead of dealing with problems in the here and now, the Liberals tend to cut a cheque and kick the problems down the road. The Liberals hand out cheques to help Canadians pay prices they cannot bring down. Families want to be able to live on their wages, just as businesses want to make a living by selling their products, not by relying on subsidies. No one wants to have to wait around for a government cheque just to make ends meet.

I want to turn now to the Alto project, the much-touted high-speed rail link. In the budget, the Liberals present Alto as a major driver of economic growth. I have a very simple question: Where are the studies proving that? Where is the evidence that this project will be profitable? Which independent study proves it? Where is the proof that taxpayers will recoup their investment? Where are the guarantees that costs will not spiral out of control?

The Parliamentary Budget Officer has already estimated construction costs at between $75 billion and $113 billion. Those are staggering figures. I doubt that those amounts are fully reflected in the current budget. This is taxpayers' money: money from workers, farmers, small business owners and families who pay their taxes. The government already seems eager to fast-track the project.
Annex 3 of the budget states:

Quote.QuotePara: In Budget 2026, the government proposes to introduce new legislation that will support accelerating the construction of Alto High-Speed Rail. Legislation will streamline expropriation activities and enable early preconstruction work.

Content.ParaText: The government is going to accelerate the expropriation process. Something is really off. The government really wants to accelerate expropriations and start pre-construction work. It wants to move the project forward. It is not even hiding it. However, serious questions remain unanswered. Is it cost-effective? Do Canadians really need it? Have the economic benefits been confirmed as announced? The government wants to accelerate the process, but it has yet to answer all of these questions.

In the meantime, farmers and property owners are in limbo, unsure whether the project could affect their land and property. I am thinking especially of farmers in the Mirabel area, who already survived one expropriation for the former airport. Today, they are in limbo once again. These people deserve answers. They deserve to be heard.

Now let us talk about bureaucracy. That is probably where the expectations were the highest and the disappointment is the greatest. The Minister of Finance set the bar very high. He talked about streamlining administrative procedures. Small and medium-sized businesses were expecting concrete action. Business owners on the ground do not need to be told what bureaucracy is. They experience it every day. Owners of garages, farms, restaurants and construction firms want to keep their businesses running. They spend too much of their days filling out forms, meeting the requirements of various government departments and trying to understand rules that keep changing. They want to run a business, not become experts in federal red tape. What does the budget actually offer them? It offers them a tax deduction for investments that was previously announced. That is all.

After the Minister of Finance set expectations so high, where is the big plan to streamline administrative procedures? Where are the concrete measures to cut red tape? Where is the plan to eliminate redundancies and unnecessary requirements? I will say it again: This budget is all sizzle and no steak.

The government announced major changes. Canadians were promised a real transformation. In the end, business owners are finding that there are very few new measures. We cannot ask businesses to be more productive while also forcing them to waste hours and days dealing with the federal bureaucracy. We need to trust them. We need to give them space to work and create wealth.

When we put all these things together, we can see why this budget is so underwhelming. We have a government that continues to rack up deficits. We have an interest bill that will be $25.3 billion a year higher by 2030-31. We have families who are seeing their purchasing power decline and who are being offered temporary cheques instead of lasting solutions. We have a high-speed project with a price tag in the tens of billions of dollars but whose benefits have yet to be proven and for which the government already wants to speed up expropriations. We have provinces calling for more resources to care for their citizens.

Canadians work hard. They get up early in the morning. They pay their taxes. They deserve better than promises and announcements. They deserve a government that spends prudently, respects taxpayer dollars and tackles the real issues. With this budget, unfortunately, Canadians may once again be paying a lot to get very little in return.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Caroline Desrochers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, my colleague talked about affordability. I know that he is keenly aware that housing is the number one expense for a household. Budget 2026 invests $45 billion in improving the housing supply to tackle all the housing-related issues. This includes recapitalizing Build Canada Homes to build even more affordable housing.

We are maintaining the existing programs that support tens of thousands of projects currently under construction, such as the CMHC programs, the infrastructure investments to help build more housing, and the red tape reduction measures. Obviously, the centrepiece of this budget is the investment to end homelessness in 10 years.
I wonder if my colleague can confirm that investing in housing is clearly good for Canadians and good for Quebeckers.

Mr. Speaker, I hear my colleague promoting the Liberal budget. Yesterday, I heard the Minister of Finance promoting his budget as energetically as a 1960s vacuum cleaner salesman. Remember the big Electrolux vacuum cleaner that was supposed to suck up all the dust? With this budget, the government is sucking up all the money out of Canadians' wallets.
The Liberals certainly have convinced us that they are the masters of our destiny.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on the fact that the budget once again includes oil and gas subsidies and also provides for the creation of a so-called sovereign wealth fund, which is anything but sovereign, to fund major projects such as the proposed oil sands pipeline on the west coast. That pipeline would carry one million barrels of oil a day and cost at least $43 billion, much of which will be public funding.
Does my colleague think that this budget is good for the environment?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure my colleague agrees with me. Under the new provision of Bill C-39, the government is giving itself the power to start major projects without waiting for the results of the environmental assessment. It will look at the recommendations after, and then it might do something about them, or it might not. Basically, the government is just doing whatever it wants.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for the great concern he shows for Quebeckers, as well as Canadians.

I wonder if he could share some of his thoughts on this incredibly massive amount of added debt for Canadians. The budget shows over $60 billion, but the reality is the cash out the door for this year is going to be about $154 billion. About $90 billion of that money is actually hidden as capital. We will have an extra $154 billion just this year and almost three quarters of a trillion dollars added over the next five years.
What does my colleague think it is going to do to his kids, his grandkids and future generations of Quebeckers and Canadians as they have to pay this back?
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for his very thoughtful question.

I am worried too. I am worried about what life will be like for my children and especially for my grandchildren. The budget's projections extend as far as 2060. In 2060, my grandchildren will be paying for today's disastrous budget and its long-term consequences.
Five years from now, we will already be paying $85 billion a year. What will it be 10 or 15 years from now? Will we be spending $100 billion or $125 billion on debt payments alone?
Think of what this money could have done for our grandchildren's future.
Mr. Speaker, I salute my colleague. We serve together on the Standing Committee on Official Languages.

The budget includes $400 million for the Francophonie summit. We are continuing to implement our official languages action plan, which is backed by a $4.1-billion investment. This is the largest investment in official languages in history. Culture is receiving $4 billion, which will have benefits for Canada's francophonie. Next year's francophone immigration target is 9.5%, setting francophone communities back on the path to growth.
Is my colleague as excited as I am about what yesterday's budget does for Canada's francophonie?
Mr. Speaker, I am excited about anything that supports the francophonie, particularly if it means conducting an economic study to examine the benefits of the Canadian francophonie around the world.

Mr. Speaker, the government talks about elbows up, Canada strong, building Canada strong, spending less to invest more, it being time to build, building a Canada people can afford, the strongest economy in the G7, a new Liberal government, the best possible deal for Canadians, building together, the true North strong and free, giving ourselves far more than the Americans can take away, and the idea that no deal is better than a bad deal. Now it talks about being masters of our destiny.

The government by sound bite is killing us. We have got to get past this and actually get to some serious governance in the House of Commons and across the country as well. This is just complete inanity going forward.

Budgets are documents about choices the government has to make going forward about how it balances society's interests. The Liberals have turned from those actual budgets to tome-sized documents about all the great things they are going to do for Canadians. In that actual revolution of what the document was supposed to be and what it has become for the sound bite-obsessed Liberals on the other side of the House has been just nuts. There are 510 pages of what they want to do, and about how they are going to be all things to all people. It is just a bunch of words the Liberals put together to try to impress a whole bunch of people and get some special interests onside.

I know that there are a whole bunch of things in the budget for a whole bunch of people all the way across the country, and businesses are going to jump at the chance, because we are becoming much less of a democratic society and much more of a government-knows-best, centrally planned economy society. I think there are a lot of people who, if they take a look at that long-term, are going to actually worry about where it started and how we got here. It is escalating, and we notice the way the government is actually moving further in this direction.

The thing about budgets is that they are sacred documents about choices we have to make going forward, no matter where we are. It lays out the things we can do and the things we cannot do. However, the Liberal government has consistently shown that it has not had to pay the price for ramping up deficit after deficit. That is the way it has been since 2015, when it was supposed to run short deficits for a short period of time. At that point in time, Canadians were still of the mind that the government had to balance the budget. There is a reckoning at some point in time for spending tomorrow's taxpayers' dollars today.

I am sure members will recall when the Liberals under former prime minister Jean Chrétien had to make a fundamental choice for Canadians. They had to cut health care funding and university funding across Canada. It used to be that 50¢ per dollar was paid by the federal government, before the mid-1990s when the Chrétien government had to make extreme cuts in order to get back to balance. The International Monetary Fund had said that the Canadian government could no longer pay its bills and could risk not being able to pay even the interest on its bills, which had escalated to about 40% of our collective taxes at that point in time. The Liberals had to make severe tax cuts very quickly, and that meant they stopped transferring funds to the provinces.

It was the easy way to do it. That was the biggest federal expenditure. There is an overlap between what the provinces should pay for and what the federal government should pay for. The Chrétien Liberals made the unsavoury decision they had to make: They cut the spending they gave to provinces. As a result, our health care system faltered. The provinces had to spend more of their resources on health care over the next decade in order to try to deliver a health care system that Canadians used to be able to count on.

That is about choices. We have to recognize where these choices have to go. It is not about being all things to all people. The cost of this is billions of dollars foisted upon a different generation. Literally, now it is hundreds of billions of dollars.

Let me explain that, because it is not immediately clear in the budget what the Liberals have done. The Prime Minister is very financially astute. He has played around with balance sheets and income statements in his previous life. Now he is doing that with the Government of Canada, the Government of Canada's balance sheet and the Government of Canada's income statement. The Liberal government and the previous Liberal government came up with several debt metrics along the way, such as the debt-to-GDP ratio and the deficit-to-GDP ratio. It kept missing these targets all along the way. If the Liberals are going to keep missing their targets, their so-called anchors, the best thing to do is to change the definitions of what those anchors are.

If we look at what we actually carry in debt in this country right now, we see that there is interest-bearing debt outstanding for Canada, over $1.5 trillion that we owe debt on around the world. That is just the Government of Canada. The provincial governments owe a lot more as well, but more than $1.5 trillion is owed, and we pay interest on that. Currently we are paying about $60 billion a year of interest on the more than $1.5 trillion of interest-paying debt. That is going to go up over the next five years by $765 billion.

The government can talk about investing versus operational deficits. That is garbage. There is and always has been a way to account for this. The Liberals are obfuscating the fact that they are going to increase the country's borrowings on international markets by 50% over the next five years and pay interest on that, with 85.5 billion taxpayer dollars going toward interest. That is obscene. To try to hide that in the budget document by changing the definitions is chicanery of the highest order. I call out the government on that because the Liberals have to be more transparent with Canadians about what they are actually causing for future generations of Canadians. The government is spending like there is no tomorrow.

I am going to give an example. According to the spring economic update, the amount the government is going to have to borrow over the next five years was only $668 billion. Since then, that number has gone up by almost $100 billion, which we in this country are going to have to borrow and pay interest on. Do we think this is a problem, including going forward, when we are not going to be able to pay our interest on the amount that is outstanding, which Canadians owe on the world markets?

I do not know what the endgame is here for the Liberals, but we are piling unsustainable debt onto Canadians' backs. I hear my colleagues across the way talk about how there is a crisis in the world so we have to spend like there is no tomorrow. I have been a member of the House for seven years, and I cannot say how many times the Liberals have said that we need to blow our brains out because there is a crisis.

There have been two legitimate crises in the last two decades: the financial crisis in 2008 and the pandemic we went through, but now the Liberals are addicted to throwing money out the door, and they continue to throw it out the door more and more. There are always good reasons to throw money at people. The people receiving it think it is a great thing. However, the people spending it are not going to be happy when they get the bill at the end of the day, when it becomes more transparent about what actually is being spent and how they are not going to be able to pay the bills down the road, the taxes that future generations of Canadians have to pay. That is the price the government is exacting from Canadians at this point in time.

I am going to talk a little about democracy. Democracy matters in this country. My colleague referred earlier to how the government continues to roll this out the door. The budget that was just presented is the budget for 2026-27, a fiscal year that ends in five months. That is great. The Liberals have just given us a budget seven months late. They are seven months late to deliver a budget for the current fiscal year.

This is not normal. The Liberals pretended this was normal coming out of an election, but this is not normal for the way the country is to run. Throughout the summer and throughout the intervening period, the government has spun money out and has made announcement after announcement, and now a bunch of that money-spinning appears in the budget. This is not democracy. This is not the way one sets a budget for Canadians and gets it passed in the House of Commons.

All those announcements the Liberals made all through the summer, where they chucked money out the door, are now in a budget that says this is what they are going to spend this year. As I say, the spring economic update said we would have to borrow an additional $668 billion over five years. They now finally present the budget, and it is $775 billion to borrow over the next five years, a ludicrous amount of money. Again, though, there are no anchors, no guardrails whatsoever. It is a government with no guidelines whatsoever. It just wants to spend money.

There has to be an end to this. I hope that end happens before Canadians realize that they are at the end of their rope, because many Canadians are at the end of their rope financially, and that we actually get some sanity back into the way we deliver the finances of this country.

Mr. Speaker, in the budget, there is a $400-million investment to optimize energy efficiency for Canadian industrial manufacturing facilities. It is called SHIFT, the strategic high-efficiency industrial facilities transition program.

The member for Calgary Centre introduced a private member's bill, Bill C-269, which calls for a tax credit for heat recovery equipment to recover heat produced by industrial processes. I am curious if the member for Calgary Centre supports our government's $400-million investment in SHIFT.

Mr. Speaker, I was going to ask the member that question earlier today, because just two days ago the Liberals voted down the actual credit that we talked about here, and it was well costed, it was supported by industry and it was actually very clear about what it was doing.

This shift is a bit of a mirage. The budget just tossed $400 million out there, but it does not explain exactly what they are going to do. The problem, as with all the things the government is doing at this point in time, is that the government is going to pick and choose who its friends are. That is who is going to get the projects of national interest. Someone is going to have to have friends in the Prime Minister's Office.
As I said in my speech, it has become a much more centrally controlled economy, as opposed to a private sector-driven economy that follows the rules.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague said that this will not end well if we do not get this under control. I wonder if he could just project a bit. If the spending does not come under control, if we have another budget like this one next year and if we continue to simply spend this way, how would this end? Could he project what would happen if the government does not bring its spending under control?

Mr. Speaker, there are many scenarios that people put on the table. Canada is, believe it or not, one of the most indebted countries in the world. There are three types of debt: corporate, individual and government. In that hierarchy, Canada is the second-most indebted country in the world, behind only Luxembourg. We should think about that, because eventually, at the end of the day, there is one taxpayer: the Canadian taxpayer. They have a mortgage and consumer debt. There is a whole bunch of corporate debt that gets passed down to consumers, and there is a whole bunch of government debt that lands on the backs of consumers as well, who are paying the interest on each of those.

That is heavier in Canada than almost anywhere else in the world. It is something that is going to land on the backs of taxpayers. I do not know what the government is going to use as a backstop at some point in time, but this is unsustainable. Effectively, the government is going to have to look at assets and what it is going to have to deal with, with the International Monetary Fund, at some point in time in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on something. How is it possible that a government can find a way to spend more money, much more than before, while cutting funding to the provinces and Quebec, particularly with regard to health transfers?
It makes no sense. Our residents need care and our hospitals need renovations. We did not ask for transfers to be increased. We simply asked that they be maintained.
The government has even shown a certain degree of contempt, going so far as to cut them. I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on that.

Mr. Speaker, that is an important question. Looking at the budget, I noticed that government's personal income tax revenues will increase by more than 4% per year over the next five years. However, its spending on health care is only going to increase by 3%. The government will be receiving more revenue from individuals, but it will be spending less on health care. Where is that money going?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Sherry Romanado (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I did listen carefully to my colleague's speech, and I have one question for him. In budget 2026, we also include $25 million for the military and civilians who were injured at CFB Wainwright, in addition to another $3 million. Would the member support that initiative?

Mr. Speaker, yes, of course I will. We have to take good care of our military, especially at this point in time, just before Remembrance Day. I thank my colleague for her government's putting forward the support for all the people who serve our country so well.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in this place just before we go to our constituencies.

As to the last exchange between the hon. parliamentary secretary and my friend from Calgary Centre, we are all mindful of the losses in our military, particularly from the disaster that just happened at CFB Wainwright. There are things that we share in this place, and I hope one of them is eternal gratitude for our veterans and those who serve in the armed forces.
Once we leave this place today, we will be back in our own constituencies for one week, so this opportunity to speak to the budget I really appreciate.

Last year, I struggled with the 2025 budget. I discussed it with members of the Prime Minister's staff, with the Prime Minister and with the former minister of the environment, and in the end, I was the only opposition member to vote for it. I do not think this is a spoiler alert, but that will not be happening again. I will not be voting for this budget. I am appalled, on numerous levels, by the budget.

There is much that has been said in this place that I do not need to repeat. The member for Vancouver East was speaking to her concerns. Yes, it is good to see the commitment to end homelessness, but where are the funds going to be found to ensure that first nations, Inuit and Métis people have adequate housing?

I completely agree with my friend from Calgary Centre and my friend from Wellington—Halton Hills North that this budget is miraculously weird. The Government of Canada can insist that other entities live up to generally acceptable accounting practices, but apparently it does not have to live up to them itself.

Given that I have a limited amount of time, I want to speak to the fundamental reason that I am grievously shocked by how bad this budget. There is one key topic, one thing, that I want to focus on in the time I have available: This is the first budget in more than a decade that not only fails to live up to the challenge of the climate crisis, but actually repudiates the very idea of targets.

On page 7 of the budget, it attacks the idea of targets. For Canadians who are watching, it says, “For too long, climate action was about targets without a practical plan”. Then it refers to investments as “punitive regulations”. Then it says, “Our new approach is a bold, pragmatic plan with four pillars”. None of them take us anywhere near the targets.

I want to make it very clear to anyone watching that the targets repudiated in this budget are legally binding. Canada signed on to them under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, to which we are a party, and through which we committed that when we tabled a target, we were committed to achieving it. That target, the current one to which Canada is legally committed, is for significant reductions by 2030.

A previous government under Stephen Harper left in place its targets for 2030. In this place, at least the Liberals, New Democrats, the Bloc and the Greens had said that what Stephen Harper's former minister of environment, Leona Aglukkaq, had tabled was woefully insufficient. We are not going to even meet those targets now, much less the improved targets that Justin Trudeau put in place.

Why does this matter? It is all fine to hear the verbiage over and again that the world has changed and that everything has changed, but guess what has not changed. Canada is still located on planet earth. We are still subject to what happens in the planetary atmosphere, to physics and to the chemistry of the atmosphere, which we have already changed through our conduct.

We know from the world's best scientists and the world's most extensive peer review process, called the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, that if we do not reduce emissions very drastically, and before 2030, we are in for an accelerated heating of the planet that would cost, as it has already cost Canadians, billions of dollars in insurable losses and uninsurable losses, like the loss of life and loss of species. The heat dome in British Columbia in 2021 that killed 619 people in four days also killed three billion sea creatures in that same time, four days.

We cannot ignore the climate crisis, yet that is what this budget does. The Liberals still mouth the words “net zero by 2050” as if they are meaningful. They are not consistent with the science. They are not part of the Paris Agreement. Net zero by 2050 was an invention for public relations purposes to kick down the road to 2050 any real action for our children and grandchildren. As a grandmother of a two-year-old, I am not just worried but terrified for what kind of future our kids are going to have.

I voted for the budget last year because the Prime Minister stood and said the government was committed to achieving the Paris Agreement targets. I was a fool to believe the Liberals. I have repented for being a fool. I see clear-eyed now. They are building pipelines that are going to drive up emissions, and who is going to pay for them? It is the people of Canada. Is there a cost-benefit analysis? No. Will there be one? No. Why? It is because they want to drive up emissions. I do not understand why the government wants to drive up emissions and pour fuel on the fire of a climate crisis that takes Canadians' lives, destroys our crops and hurts our businesses from coast to coast. Worse, it steals the future from our children and does so in broad daylight.

This is not a budget I can vote for, and I beg the government and members who care about climate, who I know are there and care, to stand up and insist that we have climate action that does not mean building pipelines and expanding oil and gas production but reducing emissions and restoring forest cover as quickly as possible. Please do not tell us about giving $2.5 billion to De Havilland to help its bottom line. That does not buy a single water bomber for Canada. We must treat the climate crisis as the emergency that it is. We can no longer afford to hit the snooze button when the alarms—
