She said: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues for allowing third reading of Bill C-268 to begin today. This bill addresses a very real problem. There are still many regions across Canada without cellphone coverage. The map may show that there is coverage and the telecommunications contract may include coverage obligations, but on the ground, people do not get a signal on their cellphone. It is this disconnect between what we see on paper and what people are actually experiencing that led me to introduce this bill.

I began working on this issue during the election campaign, following a discussion with the mayor of Martinville, Michel‑Henri Goyette, who really opened my eyes to the cell service issues in his community. As is likely the case for all members who represent rural areas, I had experienced this problem myself. As I said when I introduced this bill, cell service is not a luxury. It is a matter of safety and economic development. It is a matter of fairness. Today, cellphones are a basic tool for working, communicating, getting around and calling for help, and yet there are still Canadians who have to leave their home and climb a hill or drive several kilometres just to make a call. That is unacceptable and needs to change.

Bill C-268 does three main things. First, it requires the CRTC to establish a process to ensure the accuracy of mobile network coverage data, because before we can solve a problem, we must first know precisely where it exists. Second, it requires the Minister of Industry to maintain and update the Spectrum Policy Framework for Canada. This framework has not been updated since 2007, the era of flip phones. Today, we have 5G networks, connected vehicles and satellites that communicate directly with our cellphones. Public policy must keep pace with technological change. Third, the bill provides for a periodic review of the framework. The objective is not to predict what technology will look like in 15 or 20 years. No one can do that. The objective is to ensure that our policies can evolve alongside technology.

I do want to highlight a positive development that has occurred since the spring. Issues related to cellular connectivity and network deployment have become much more prominent in the government's work. That is great news. Budget 2026 recognizes that challenges regarding coverage and reliability persist, particularly in rural and remote communities. The budget includes measures to release more spectrum for 5G and private networks, support satellite services that can extend coverage in rural and remote areas, update spectrum transfer rules and modernize infrastructure. I am particularly pleased to see these measures because affordability is important. However, for me, the key issue is deployment. A cheaper plan does not do much if the telephone is not connected in the first place.

Improving coverage requires proper rules, good spectrum management, reliable coverage data and investments. My bill is part of that process. I want to thank the researchers who helped shape the bill, Matthew McNally and Gregory Taylor. I also want to thank Michel‑Henri Goyette and the mayors in my riding who have continued to raise awareness of the realities on the ground and ensure that these issues are heard in Ottawa as much as they are now. Above all, I would like to thank my colleagues from all parties, because this bill is a good example of what we can accomplish when we focus on the problem rather than on our political differences.

Cell connectivity is not a Liberal, Conservative, NDP, Bloc or Green issue. It is an issue that concerns everyone. When a firefighter is out of reach on a country road, the problem remains the same, regardless of political affiliation. When a farm operation loses its connection, the problem remains the same, regardless of political affiliation. When a family has to drive a few kilometres away to make a call, the problem remains the same, regardless of political affiliation.

I am truly grateful for the support that the bill has received so far. For a private member's bill introduced in March to have reached third reading by November is remarkably fast. Above all, it shows a willingness to work together. I hope that our collaboration will continue through to the end. If my colleagues wish to keep moving the bill forward and send it to the Senate, I already someone in the other place who is prepared to sponsor it. I sincerely thank Senator Réjean Aucoin, who told me that he would take up the bill if it reaches the Senate. I am very grateful to him for that.

Our goal is not simply to pass a law. Our goal is that one day, folks everywhere, from Martinville, Quebec, to Chéticamp, Nova Scotia, to Whitehorse, Yukon, or any community in Canada, will be able to pick up their phones on a road where they used to lose the signal and see that the problem has finally been fixed. That is what I want, and that is why I am asking my colleagues to keep working together to move Bill C-268 forward.
Mr. Speaker, this is legislation we are supportive of, and we are looking forward to further discussion.

I did want to take this opportunity, though, and it relates to spectrum, the opportunities people are going to have and how people see their future, to ask the member to comment on the jobs report that came out today, because we have not heard from any member of the government on the jobs report. We repeatedly asked about it in question period, but heard no response on it. The 50,000 jobs lost in the private sector and a big increase in youth unemployment are the results we are seeing.
The government, understandably, I think, does not want to talk about it, but can the member share any reaction to what we saw released from Statistics Canada today?

Mr. Speaker, cellular connectivity is essential to our economic development. Businesses need this connectivity to be able to operate. Sometimes technical issues prevent them from moving forward, getting new contracts and continuing to grow. Expanding cellular connectivity is one way to support the employability of people and the growth of businesses in the regions. I see it as an essential tool for economic development.

Right now, some farmers cannot use new technologies. Shipping companies are struggling to communicate. By improving cellular connectivity, we will help businesses be more successful and create good jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my friend and colleague from Compton—Stanstead for her strong advocacy on behalf of her constituency. She is incredible, and I have a great deal of respect for her.
Can she give us some examples of the economic consequences of poor connectivity in rural areas, particularly when it comes to cellphone service?

Mr. Speaker, yes, there are significant economic impacts on businesses. While Internet access is steadily improving, cellular coverage remains a challenge. Transportation provides a clear example of the difficulties we face. The agricultural sector is also feeling the effects.

Students may be unable to complete assignments remotely due to a lack of connectivity. This has economic consequences, and social ones as well. Telehealth is still not an option in certain regions. This is also a matter of public safety. There are firefighters who cannot call for backup. There are people on the road who cannot contact emergency services after an accident. This really does create dangerous situations. In our area, some people cannot call 911.

Furthermore, as my riding borders the U.S., some residents pick up a signal from the United States. When they dial 911, their call is routed to a U.S. dispatch centre. It can take a very long time before they are transferred back to Canada. Public safety is of the utmost importance to me.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for bringing forward this bill and for her remarks. Coming from a rural riding, I know all the dead spots when I am driving, so I know when I am going to hang up before the call simply drops. That is on the highway. When a combine light is on fire and someone cannot call 911, that is a real problem. I have communities that I can stand in the middle of and not be able to make a phone call whatsoever. It is absurd. The telecom companies' maps say that we have perfect coverage, and they are lying. It is a complete facade.

In the last budget that was tabled yesterday, I scanned through to find out what more could be done. I think this legislation is an important step to provide transparency in the mapping. In the budget itself, though, I saw nothing substantial that is going to lead to actual improvements in wireless coverage for my communities.

Mr. Speaker, in my remarks, I did say that I was very pleased to see this mentioned in the budget. This proves that the government is very concerned about this issue. The budget mentions the issue of connectivity in rural and remote areas, as well as the affordability of telecommunications services. The proposed solutions that will be implemented are more spectrum for 5G networks and private networks, and satellite services. Satellites are the future.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today at third reading of Bill C-268, an act respecting the spectrum policy framework for Canada. I would like to thank the member for Compton—Stanstead for bringing this legislation before Parliament and for her efforts in advancing this important discussion.

As Conservatives indicated at second reading, we support the objective of improving accountability and transparency in how wireless coverage is measured and how spectrum policy is reviewed in Canada. After hearing the testimony presented before the Standing Committee on Industry and Technology, Conservatives continue to support this bill, and we believe it is a constructive step in the right direction. That said, I believe it is important that we be honest with Canadians about what the bill could and could not accomplish.

In 2007, smart phones were only beginning to emerge. Streaming services were in their infancy. Remote work was relatively uncommon. Cloud computing was not yet part of everyday life for most Canadians. Artificial intelligence was largely the subject of academic research rather than a tool used by businesses and consumers every day. Today, virtually every aspect of modern life depends on connectivity. Our businesses depend upon it. Our educational institutions depend upon it. Our health care systems depend upon it.

Bill C-268 would not eliminate every dead zone. It would not immediately bring cell service to every kilometre of highway. It would not instantly connect every rural and remote community. However, it would address a fundamental question that Parliament should always be asking, which is whether we are measuring success accurately.

Too often in Ottawa, governments become preoccupied with targets, statistics, maps and announcements. Canadians, on the other hand, judge success much differently. Canadians judge success when they pick up their phone and it works. They judge success when they can call for help, as my colleague from Portage—Lisgar said. They judge success when they can operate a business, connect with customers and communicate with family members.

That gap between what governments report and what Canadians experience in their daily lives was a recurring theme throughout the committee's study of this legislation. Witnesses acknowledged that there can be a difference between coverage that exists on paper and coverage that is actually experienced in the real world.

For many Canadians, particularly those living outside major urban centres, that reality is all too familiar. They have all experienced it. A coverage map indicates service is available. A government report indicates objectives are being met. A telecommunications provider states an area is covered, yet when Canadians attempt to make a call, send a message or access emergency services, they discover that reality does not quite match the map.

The demand for reliable connectivity has increased exponentially, yet the framework that guides Canada's spectrum policy has remained largely unchanged. It is entirely reasonable for Parliament to insist that such an important framework be reviewed on a regular basis. In fact, Conservatives argued at committee that reviews should take place every two years instead of every five years.

Technology evolves rapidly. Markets evolve rapidly. Consumer expectations evolve rapidly. We believe that more frequent reviews would have better reflected the pace of technological change. Unfortunately, that amendment was defeated. Nevertheless, the principle remains the same, which is that regular review is better than no review.

While much of this debate is focused on rural and remote communities, I would like to discuss why this matter is also important to the people I represent in Calgary Centre. Calgary Centre is an urban constituency. It is home to office towers, entrepreneurs, financial institutions, technology start-ups and thousands of highly skilled professionals. At first glance, it may appear that connectivity challenges affecting rural Canada are far removed from the lives of those living and working in downtown Calgary. Nothing could be further from the truth. Calgary's prosperity is deeply connected to what happens beyond city limits.

The engineers who design energy infrastructure in Calgary often oversee projects operating hundreds of kilometres away. The geologists evaluating resource opportunities rely on data generated from remote locations across Alberta. Energy companies monitor pipelines, facilities and operations spread across vast areas of Western Canada. Construction firms, transportation companies and service providers routinely operate in areas where connectivity remains unreliable.

Workers travel these roads every day. Truck drivers travel these roads every day. Tradespeople travel these roads every day. Families travel these roads every day. All of them expect a basic level of connectivity and safety. In many respects, connectivity has become just as important to modern commerce as roads, railways and airports. Without it, economic activity becomes more difficult, less efficient and less competitive.

This is particularly true for Alberta's energy sector. The energy industry is increasingly reliant on sophisticated communications technologies, real-time data, remote monitoring systems and advanced automation. Reliable connectivity supports productivity, efficiency and safety. It helps workers communicate. It helps operators monitor critical infrastructure. It helps businesses compete in a global economy. It helps ensure that Canadian resources can continue contributing to our national prosperity.

When people think about connectivity, they often think about convenience: the ability to browse the Internet, the ability to stream a video and the ability to check emails. Those things certainly matter. However, connectivity today is also an essential economic tool. For energy producer monitoring facilities in rural Alberta, connectivity is not a luxury. For a business serving clients across multiple regions, connectivity is not a luxury. For a worker travelling to a remote site, connectivity is not a luxury. It is infrastructure.

There is another aspect of this legislation that deserves attention, and that is public safety. Perhaps the most compelling argument for improving coverage accuracy and accountability is the impact that connectivity has on emergency response. When Canadians find themselves in distress, they need confidence that they can call for help. That expectation should not depend on a postal code. It should not depend on whether someone happens to be driving along a major urban corridor or a more remote stretch of highway. It should not depend on whether someone lives in a large city or a small community.

Across Canada, we have witnessed floods, wildfires, severe storms and other emergencies that have demonstrated the importance of reliable communications infrastructure. First responders depend on communications systems to coordinate their response. Families depend on communications systems to receive alerts and information. Individuals depend on communications systems to seek assistance. When connectivity fails, the consequences can be significant. That is why accountability matters. That is why transparency matters. That is why accurate information matters. Canadians deserve to know whether coverage claims actually reflect real-world outcomes.

I often say that effective public policy starts with a simple principle: tell Canadians the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. If there is a coverage gap, we need to identify it. If there is a problem, we need to acknowledge it. If objectives are not being met, we need to be honest about it. Only then can meaningful solutions be developed.

Bill C-268 would help move us in that direction. It would create a mechanism for better verification. It would require regular review. It would provide greater transparency. It would give Parliament additional tools to assess whether policies are delivering the outcomes that Canadians expect.

Would this bill solve every problem? No. Would it eliminate every dead zone? No. Would it instantly close every connectivity gap across this vast country? No. However, it would make it harder for governments and regulators to rely solely on paper success when Canadians are experiencing something entirely different on the ground. For Conservatives, that is an important principle. Governments should be judged on results, not aspirations, not announcements and not press releases, but results.

At the end of the day, Canadians do not care what a coverage map says if their phone cannot place a call. They do not care what percentage appears in a government report if they lose service on the highway. They do not care how success is defined in Ottawa if they cannot connect when it matters most.

Canadians deserve reliable service. Canadians deserve accurate information. Canadians deserve accountability. Canadians deserve a spectrum policy framework that is periodically reviewed to ensure that it remains relevant in a rapidly changing technological environment.
For those reasons, Conservatives will be supporting Bill C-268 at third reading, and I encourage all members of the House to do the same.

I see that some members are rising expecting questions and comments, but this is, of course, third reading of a private member's bill. This is a good moment to explain that in the first hour of third reading, only the mover of the motion has the right to speak, and then they get five minutes of questions and comments. In the second hour, the same mover of the motion will end with a right of reply. In this case, it is her choice whether or not to take it, but it will only be in the second hour.
Resuming debate.
The member for Berthier—Maskinongé.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased speak to Bill C-268. That said, I am going to take the liberty of making a brief aside right at the outset. I am sure my colleagues will not mind.

I was a high school teacher for 25 years. Yesterday, I found out that a former colleague of mine, a teacher at L'Érablière high school who inspired me greatly and whom I hold in high regard, has won a science teaching award known as the Raymond Gervais Award. Charline Liard-Arbour is radiant, bubbly, full of energy, and, above all, innovative. She always has fresh ideas for making her subject more engaging, and I think this accolade is fully deserved. I tip my hat to her.

I would now like to come back to today's topic, Bill C-268. I am pleased to discuss it. It addresses an issue that is extremely important to everyone, but especially to members from rural ridings like mine. It is an issue that constituents bring up with us at least once a week. Cell service dead zones can pop up in surprising places. They happen everywhere. That is the truth.

When we look at Bill C-268, the first question that comes to mind is whether it will really make a difference. In committee, witnesses told us that the verifications introduced by the bill are already being carried out. One thing is certain: This bill will make reviews and transparency mandatory. This bill will force the government to update the spectrum policy framework for Canada every five years. That has not been done since 2007, so it has been awhile.

Second, it will force the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission to verify the accuracy of the coverage data provided by telecommunications companies for the regions. I think that is a really good idea.

Lastly, it will require the Minister of Industry to publish a report within 18 months of Bill C‑268 coming into force. I hope that will be done. I hope the government will honour its commitment to publish the report. There needs to be transparency.

There are also other laws, like the Foreign Interference and Security of Information Act, that are supposed to be reviewed in the first year following a general election. The last I heard, that has not yet been done. We know that even if there is an obligation to prepare a report or a study, it does not always happen. We sincerely hope that is not the case, but we have our doubts. The bill tabled by the member for Compton—Stanstead is full of good intentions. I know her well enough to believe that she wants to see action on this file. We will agree to fully support the bill. It is outrageous that, in 2026, the safety of some citizens is at risk because they do not have access to a network. That is crazy.

I have been an MP for seven years, but I have been talking about this issue for eight years. I was active in the community before I was elected. Several places have dead zones, including Saint‑Édouard‑de‑Maskinongé, Saint‑Mathieu‑du‑Parc, Saint‑Élie‑de‑Caxton and even Pointe‑du‑Lac. For those who may not know, Pointe-du-Lac is part of the city of Trois‑Rivières. Even Pointe‑du‑Lac has dead zones.

Sometimes, people can encounter problems in urban or semi-urban areas too, like Saint‑Boniface, Saint‑Étienne‑des‑Grès, Saint‑Alexis‑des‑Monts, Sainte‑Geneviève‑de‑Berthier, Saint‑Gabriel‑de‑Brandon and Saint‑Didace.

As elected officials, especially at the federal level, if we want to have a presence in our communities, we have to be mobile. We spend a lot of time in our cars. What do people do while sitting in their car? They do admin. Through the magic of Bluetooth technology, people can talk on the phone. We know where the dead zones are. In the middle of a conversation with someone, we will warn them that a dead zone is coming up ahead, that our call might drop and we might have to call them back. That is not normal. It may be a funny example, but it can be a very serious problem if a driver gets in an accident on an isolated stretch of road and calling for help is not an option. In my riding, some deaths could have been prevented. This has not been proven, but sadly, by all indications, these deaths could have been avoided had there been signal. That is sad.

It is the government's responsibility to do everything it can to improve the situation. As elected officials, we are working hard and we want this to work, but government structures like the CRTC need to address this.

Licence holders must be compelled to use the spectrum. Some companies pay to reserve spectrum, but do not develop it. They do not believe it is profitable enough. I think the government should be able to say that, if they bought the spectrum, they have to develop it, and then give them a very short time frame to do so. If that spectrum is not developed, too bad for the licence holder. They will have to give it up and pass it on to the next operator. At some point, we need to ensure coverage for our population. The way it is makes no sense.

I imagine that my colleague is thrilled about our support. Sometimes things get rusty over time. The bill talks about implementing a review mechanism and requiring a report. Members can count on us to demand those reports. I urge my colleague to speak with the Minister of Industry and tell her that she will have to produce results, because we want to see results, output and new towers built where they are needed. If there are any companies that are waiting to make more profit, if they are not developing the spectrum or if they are refusing to share towers, as we sometimes see, that is unacceptable. We need to take action on that.
The Bloc Québécois will enthusiastically support this bill, in the hope that it will improve the situation.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to speak on a subject of great importance in my constituency: cellular connectivity. This is an issue that worries me, just as it worries my colleague, the member for Compton—Stanstead, who is also a very strong advocate for the vitality of rural areas.

In my riding, I lose signal when I am in Upper Madawaska. Then, if I move around a bit, the signal comes back. When I pass through Saint-Hilaire, I lose the connection again. It comes back again when I reach Edmundston. However, it is not so great in Saint-Basile anymore, even though it used to work a few years ago. If I keep going towards Rivière-Verte and Sainte-Anne, there are dead zones. The same happens if I go to the Restigouche area, whether I am in Balmoral, McKendrick, Glen Levit or Robinsonville, to name but a few places.

My riding has very poor cellular connectivity. This is a top concern for my constituents, so it is a priority for me as well. It is very rare that I do not hear about this issue when I go home to my riding on the weekend. It is also a priority for local elected officials, including mayors and municipal councillors. I hear about this a lot. That is why I am pleased to co-sponsor my colleague's bill, which calls for a review of Canada's spectrum policy framework with a view to promoting the deployment of cellular connectivity in rural areas.

I like to use all the platforms I have, including this speech in the House, to raise the issue of cellular connectivity in Ottawa. I am also fortunate to be the co-vice-chair of our party's rural caucus, and this issue is top of mind for our group. Since I was elected, I have had multiple meetings with telecommunications companies, including service providers, as well as companies in the new technology sector. Some of them show great potential, particularly in low-earth orbit satellite technology. These technologies have the potential to be a real game changer in terms of connectivity. Yes, we have towers to serve areas that are more densely populated, but these satellite technologies would help bridge the gap in regions that are currently underserved. Coverage in these areas could be improved using these technologies. There is no question that further regulatory adjustments are needed to really take full advantage of the potential of these new technologies. As a member of Parliament, I urge members to act quickly on this issue, which I raise regularly.

As we know, cell connectivity has enormous consequences. It impacts public safety. When cars break down in locations without service, it can cause problems. Just think of Highway 17 at night. Sometimes, it can be even more serious, when an accident happens and immediate emergency assistance is needed. It can even be a matter of life or death. Cell connectivity is an extremely serious issue, but the broader issue of economic development is another consideration. Businesses need reliable connections. That is what attracts them to a region. Consider workers, too. A lot of people work while they are on the road these days. As an MP, when I am driving around my riding, it is not unusual for my calls to drop, forcing me to wait a bit and then call the person back. This issue affects workplace productivity, because this is an inefficient way to work. It affects the regions' ability to attract and retain residents too, because cell connectivity is not a luxury; it is an essential service that affects a person's quality of life.

As members also know, people now use their cellphones to access a wide range of services, whether health care, government services or banking, to name just a few. I would also say that this is a matter of fairness between regions. If we want to build Canada strong, we need strong rural communities, and reliable cellular coverage is essential. That is why I support Bill C-268, which calls for a review of the Canada's spectrum policy framework. This is part of the solution. The other part is to emphasize the importance of acting quickly to establish a regulatory framework that supports the growth of satellite technologies in order to improve connectivity in rural and remote areas. This is an issue I have been working on and focusing on since my election to Ottawa, because I know that progress in this area will truly make a difference for the communities I represent, for my constituents, and for businesses in Madawaska—Restigouche.

I would like to take this opportunity to acknowledge the leadership of my colleague, the member for Compton—Stanstead, who is working tirelessly on the issue of cellular connectivity. She speaks about it regularly. She regularly addresses issues affecting rural areas. As the member for Madawaska—Restigouche, I always enjoy working with her because my riding and hers face many similar challenges, and I believe that by joining forces with other members from rural areas, we can successfully advance issues in Ottawa that are important to our communities. I would say that co-sponsoring this bill is another example of the strong collaboration that I hope will continue.

Mr. Speaker, I look forward to sharing a few thoughts on Bill C-268. I do think it is important to begin by discussing the context, in terms of the economic situation of our country. This bill includes an aspiration about opportunities that can be associated with rural connectivity. As members know, we are supportive of that.

The broader context, when it comes to opportunity for Canadians, is a challenging one. Yesterday, the government announced its budget. A budget is primarily about the government making the case for the things that it wants to do and the impact that it proposes will result from its policy. It is an exposition of the government's proposals, ideas and plans.

On the other hand, today, we received the jobs report, which is a report card, an assessment based on realities in the real world of what is actually happening in the economy, and gives us a real picture of whether or not the government's plans are working. The contrast between yesterday's message and today's reality is quite striking.

Yesterday, the government talked about all the jobs it was going to create. Today, we heard the results. Here they are. More than 50,000 private sector jobs were lost in the last month alone. Those are the realities, not hypotheses about the future. We saw an increase in youth unemployment from 13% to 13.7%, and an increase in the overall unemployment rate from 6.5% to 6.7%. The unemployment rate for 55-plus went up as well. There were increases across different demographics in the unemployment rate, increasing the unemployment rate overall.

Underneath that, we see some other data points that I think are important to dwell on. Number one, it is getting harder for unemployed people to find a job. The statistics track job-finding rates. Fewer than one in five unemployed Canadians found a job in the last month. It is getting harder for people who are out of work to find a job.

Also, the Statistics Canada report today looked at financial insecurity in households. Three out of 10 Canadians are living in a financially insecure household. That is a household where people are struggling to pay for their basic needs. We have a situation where people are working hard and yet there is an increase in that financial insecurity. Adding to that is the reality that Canadians are working longer hours, which is also in the jobs report.

Canadians are less likely to be working at all. If they are working, they are working longer hours and yet they are seeing higher levels of financial insecurity. If they are unemployed, they are having a harder time than ever before of finding jobs. Now, these are the realities in our economy.

First of all, we asked about the jobs report in question period, and the government consistently refused to respond or even mention the jobs report. The Liberals want to talk about the budget. We are happy to debate the provisions of the budget, but they do not want to acknowledge the existence of the jobs report, which is the report card, the results of their policies. The jobs report shows the government is failing. The Liberals do not even want to acknowledge or talk about it, and yet we have all of these numbers that demonstrate problems. These numbers demonstrate that it is harder to find a job than ever before, that more Canadians are unemployed than in the past, that it is particularly hard for young people to start out in life and access opportunities, and that those who are working are working longer and are more likely to be dealing with financial insecurity. These are the realities that I think demonstrate that the government's approach is not as sunny as it would like to pretend it is.

Moreover, when we highlight these problems, the Liberals say, “Stop talking things down. We should be optimistic. Why are you saying negative things?” I think it is important that we speak truth and look at realities. A young person who edits their credit card statement before they give it to their parents is not doing themselves or anyone else any good. The goal of looking frankly at these realities is to try to promote concrete action to address them so that we can solve the problems our country is facing. We want to solve these problems. We want to identify problems and then propose constructive solutions to them. The government putting its head in the sand, pretending that problems do not exist and pretending that things are sunnier than they are is not going to lead to solutions to the problems.

Let us look at the jobs report. Let us talk about the frank problems it demonstrates in terms of it being harder to find a job, harder to get ahead and harder to make ends meet even for those who are working. Let us talk about those problems and then let us talk about concrete solutions.

In the lead-up to the budget, Conservatives proposed detailed, concrete solutions. A year ago, we presented a jobs plan that focused on unleashing the economy, fixing immigration, fixing training and building homes where the jobs are. There were concrete proposals associated with all of those areas of recommendation. We have not seen action from the government on any of our proposals. In fact, in many cases, it has moved in the opposite direction. We also presented five different substantial constructive proposals to support families, like working to integrate work and family life, reforms to parental leave and changes to CPP to ensure that parents are not penalized for being with their kids later on in their retirement years. These are no- or low-cost proposals that would make life substantially better for Canadians, in one case protecting families impacted by the death of a parent. It was a proposal that cost less than a $1 million a year.

The Liberals are zero for five on implementing these constructive ideas. One would think they would have seen the constructive proposals coming from the opposition on jobs and families and said, “Let us put some of them in the budget. Maybe it will be harder for the opposition to criticize the budget if we take some of their good ideas and put them in there.” However, it is oh for four on taking ideas from the jobs plan, and oh for five on taking ideas from our proposals to support families. We see today the result of their unwillingness to listen to the constructive ideas that have come forward in the House. The result is a continuing worsening situation when it comes to jobs and financial security for families.

When it comes to the issue of jobs and connectivity, which the bill deals with, in rural and remote communities, addressing connectivity gaps can contribute to opportunities for people to have employment. One of the areas we are working on regarding jobs and opportunities in remote areas is to promote the construction of housing where the jobs are. We see high levels of unemployment in certain regions, which often but not always are bigger cities, and then there are labour force needs in other places. We want to support Canadians taking Canadian jobs, and that includes having an ability to take jobs where they are.

One of the barriers that can contribute to making it harder for people to relocate for jobs and opportunity is the availability of housing. We have introduced as part of our plan a significant incentive around workforce housing construction, making it easier to build homes where the jobs are and for people to choose to locate near where jobs are. Connectivity is part of that. It is one thing that allows opportunities to grow in remote areas and makes it easier for people to make a choice to locate in a different area in order to get jobs and opportunity. Conservatives have been supportive of the bill. We have been constructive in the process. We have contributed to the work that needs to happen in the area of promoting connectivity, work that I think the government has been way behind on.

Sadly, this is existing within an overall picture in which jobs are down and the government is failing. The Liberals want us to ignore their failure and feel sunny and happy about their hopes for the future. We need to look squarely at the realities and challenges and do the work necessary to address these problems. That should include implementing the constructive solutions that we have put forward as part of our jobs plan and our plan for work and family life.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. colleague for bringing forward this bill. Hearing her speech, I imagine our ridings share some similarities insofar as the rural nature of them.

I think this bill would make a difference, and that is why Conservatives supported it at second reading. I intend to also support it today. In fact, I brought up this bill while standing in a community with residents who were asking me why they could not make a phone call right where we were standing in the middle of town.

I think this is a step. Again, I was reviewing the budget from yesterday, and I see references to things like increasing spectrum availability and having it at an auction. Now, that sort of promise is positive, although it has no associated timeline with it, which is, of course, worrisome.
Going back to when we started developing this spectrum policy, it was the very earliest days of iPhones. Things have changed so immensely in technology and the way we live our lives.

Let me outline some differences. I might be driving home today here in Ottawa, and my phone call might drop. It will be annoying for a brief second, but I will hit redial, my call will be answered, and I will pick up where I left off in my conversation, versus when I am driving down—

Speaking of connectivity, the member's mobile device can be heard, and it is making it difficult for interpreters. I would invite the member to put the device away to make the work of our interpreters easier.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying, there is good service in the big cities, and that is the key difference. We can stand in this place and make a phone call, but when I am driving down the highway heading from my home in Portage down to Winkler, I know exactly where the dead spots are. When I am on the phone, I will say, “Okay, I have to let you go. I am going to lose you here.” That is not identified on the map.
It is one thing to lose a phone call and have to pick it up a couple of minutes later or 10 kilometres later, which is worse than dropping a phone call in a city.

Where it really matters is when someone's home in a rural area has no coverage. They can buy a booster for a bit of coverage right within their own home. Another example is of someone driving a combine during harvest and, heaven forbid, there is a fire, which does happen. They try to call emergency services, hoping they might be able to get there in time to save their $1-million piece of equipment, but find that they have no service. Someone could have an invader on their property in the middle of the night in a rural area, and they hope to call emergency responders, but they leave their house and have no service.

It is one thing to be annoyed in a city when we do not have the ability to make a phone call. It is another thing to have legitimate safety concerns on farms and across rural landscapes across this country. It is unfair. We pay the same prices as anybody else buying their plans from any of these big telecom companies, and we get, at best, half the service.

In many locations, people simply more or less live without service. I can think of Elm Creek, Miami or Somerset. Standing in town feels like we are living in a third world country, yet when I pull up the maps, the coverage is perfect.
The hon. member cannot use props during a speech. He can make references to maps, but not show them or hand them around.
I will invite the member to continue.

Mr. Speaker, I will outline them. For one company, it is perfectly green with a couple of spots. For the other one, it is perfectly blue. The coverage is perfect, if I go online. That is not reality. It is not reality for thousands of my constituents. It is not reality for, I assume, hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of Canadians across this country.

Yes, the bill is a positive step. Forcing transparency upon these companies, to show the actual network service they are providing to their very highly paying customers, is the absolute minimum step we can take. I do applaud the member for bringing this forward, but I think it is time to look beyond this. Let us fix this problem.

There were efforts by Conservatives on the bill in committee to try to hasten the pace of the review from five years down to two years. I wish it had been adopted, and I hope the Senate might consider such a change to make sure there are updates to this proposal, to make sure these big telecom companies are following the letter of the law, should this plan to implement transparency actually come to light.

The other factor, with respect to our rural communities, is that we are thriving for many reasons, in many places, in many ways thanks to the entrepreneurial spirit of our people. We have so many businesses that are driving our rural economy, and more importantly Canada's, that are reliant on travel between smaller communities, whether in agriculture, manufacturing or anything else. We are yet again at another competitive disadvantage, from the business lens, when they do not have good enough service.

I recognize that if this problem were easy to fix, some government would have fixed it by now. We live in a nation where competition is something we have long dreamed of yet have never been able to achieve, frankly, in just about any of our major sectors, and particularly the telecoms, so taking this small step to make transparency emerge with the big actors here would be of value. It is frustrating that when I go close to the border, I lose service from my Canadian provider, yet an American tower will pick me up, and I will join a roaming charge service to be part of a U.S. network.

Why on earth would we allow an overlapping signal to come from the United States and allow our big telecoms to not be providing service to our border communities? These are some of our most important communities in terms of trade, and in my case agriculture, that are living with a U.S. signal as their main provider. This country needs to do better. We may not think of this sort of infrastructure as infrastructure, but it is vital infrastructure that is lagging, with tremendous disparity based on where people live.

When I go back to the map, just outside of my riding in Oak Bluff, just in the corner, there is good service. In Winnipeg, there is wonderful service. I understand that many people live in our big communities, but to charge the amounts we get charged as Canadian users of these technologies, particularly the ones who are receiving some of the poorest service we could imagine, is outrageous.

Anybody who has ever travelled internationally knows there are some countries we might not expect would have unbelievable cell phone coverage, but they do. It is remarkable that people can travel across so many places in this great nation and lose signal so many times. The Liberal government has focused time and time again on fibre and access into homes, and that is important, but in my view, the wireless networks and the shortages and lacks of coverage across so many regions are more important. This is an urgent issue. It is an urgent issue for our business community, for our families and for the safety of the people we are sent here to represent.

In the budget, there are nods to this being a problem. There is a section titled “Increasing competition in the telecommunications sector”. That is a great idea, but when I read through some of the offerings of the Liberal government, I see plans to make plans, to make promises to maybe do something.

We have suffered with Liberal government inaction on this policy file for 11 years. Not a single person in my riding would say their cell phone connectivity has gotten better. In fact, many of them tell me it has gotten worse. I think of the tower near Carman that was removed, which had everybody in the region wondering, “What happened? I used to get service here. Where did it go?”

The consultation process among these companies with the people who live, work and play across our rural landscapes is abysmal. While they simultaneously manage to say that they are enhancing services, what happens on the ground is really all that matters.

I would love every map in this country from our big telecom companies to be 100% accurate. I hope that by passing this legislation, we will force upon them the level of transparency required to come closer to achieving that. I recognize that it is difficult and is something that these companies surely do not want to do, but Canadians have a right to know that they are not getting the service they are paying a significant amount for, often $100 or more a month. It is not good enough.
I hope we can pass this legislation expeditiously and, more importantly, take steps to solve the true problems of service reaching cellphones across my riding and across this country.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to get up on behalf of Skeena—Bulkley Valley to talk about Bill C-268, which is long overdue, decades overdue. The last review was done in, I think, 2017.

That aside, we are talking about connectivity. We are talking about cellphone coverage. That is what we are really talking about. The north, in my riding, has been underserved for years, with broken promises. We are also talking about safety. I agree with that. I have heard all the speeches, but in one instance, we are talking about Highway 16, which has been referred to as the Highway of Tears, where a lot of aboriginal women go missing. The promise back then was to have 100% connectivity from Prince Rupert to Prince George. We are not even close. We have not even reached 50% of that connectivity promise.

This is not just about safety. It is about building Canada strong. In this case, I would urge the government to take a lesson from this side of the House. I know it does not like to, but it really should, because the north, especially regions like my riding, actually drives the economy of Canada, yet it does not get the services it requires to be a full, functioning, healthy economy. Connectivity has a lot to do with that.

Look at the Stewart port. It has billions of dollars of potential. The Liberals mention it when they need a photo op, but does it have good connectivity? No. Has it asked for that? Yes. Has it asked for highway upgrades? Yes, it has.

The Tahltan first nation was here just yesterday asking about connectivity so they will not have to subscribe to Starlink, a U.S. company, to provide them cell service. They also want infrastructure promises. The government has to get away from getting on the coattails of projects that already have their own momentum and look at different regions that can provide billions of dollars in investment to kick-start our economy after a 10-year period of stagnation.

The golden triangle in Tahltan territory needs connectivity and highway infrastructure. In Burns Lake, we need connectivity. We can contribute more than what we already see in the papers in places like Stewart, Tahltan, Burns Lake and even Kitimat, and especially along the Highway of Tears. That was promised decades ago. In this instance, we have to hold these big telecom companies in Canada accountable and make them do as they say and say as they do, not the other way around.
This legislation is long overdue. I really urge this House to vote in favour of it going forward.
